Under the summer sun of Belogord, a group of young students took their stipend out to a freshly built commercial district. They wanted to flair up their clothing and maybe even buy some makeup. Only after all the laughter and celebrating did they realize they had spent too much, and several the next day had to make a call home. Despite having to call home, none had to worry if they would see their families again.

Within Moscow's first reconstructed Synagogue, a sight no one inside would have believed only a year ago would ever happen again, a public Bar Mitzvah was held. Not only did the fear of their entire culture being eradicated leave their mind for that moment, but they could be happy about the future for the first time. Among the tears and laughter that followed, they danced deep into the night, knowing this was but the first of many nights.

Throughout the massive motherland, the people celebrated, danced, and sang songs many thought were lost. In a place typically thought of as a cold and unforgiving place, the people of the Federation found warmth in the passion they now had in freedom.

options.name: The torch of liberty has thawed the Motherland.

title: Our Eyes on the World
desc:
"Here you go, Stepan, make sure to get this done by tomorrow!"

Stepan looked up from his desk; the smell of coffee was still fresh in his mind. One of his colleagues placed a stack of files behind his computer as he gave a polite nod to Stepan. "Don't worry, you're gonna like this one."

Stepan smiled as he reached for his coffee mug and grabbed the first file. He almost dropped his mug in surprise. "Polish home army? Resistance contacts? Weapons shipments?"

Stepan couldn't believe what he read; it seemed like Russia had bigger plans. Freeing Poland seems like an impossible endeavour, but anything that drives Germany more up against the wall would ultimately be a victory for the free world. He grabbed another file from the stack and opened it.

The Ma clique? he thought they were under Japanese control, but it appears that's not the case, another Chinese republic? That's bound for trouble, but both China and Russia could get far together with the right people, like Stepan.

He kept reading more files; Mongolian uprisings and nomad cooperation in Ulaanbaatar, they'd gladly accept Russian help. Stepan did wonder how the Co-prosperity sphere would react to this but considering that the Federation showed its might against Germany, they would probably back down.

Armenia? That's a name he hadn't heard for a while, a nation that might have even suffered more than Russia did.

There are still some rebel groups whose fires are still burning, and Russia would provide the wood they needed.

Surely Turkey wouldn't mind.

Stepan looked at the stack and smiled; he remembers when one man repaired the Russian nation, and once again, Russia will repair other countries.

He grabbed another one as he looked down into his mug, empty.

options.name: This is going to be a long one.

title: A Russian Spring
desc:
As dawn broke over the eastern horizon, the sky was filled with a soft, pink light. Valery was already awake, pulling his black coat tighter around his body in an attempt to stave off the morning chill. His old, beaten shoes drummed awkwardly on the footpath and he could feel the cold seeping through the leather already. He just smiled, however. How could he not? There was the familiar smell of sweet flowers in the air and the jewel-like glow of fresh, green leaves. Russia was in bloom once more, and Valery swelled with joy, that he had lived to see it.

Not so long ago, any dreams of an end to occupation had seemed far-off and fragile. The very joy of life, that Valery savoured now, had been sealed under lock and key in iron freight trains and deported away into the black heart of the Reich. When the Federation had spread its wings and crossed the Reich's border, Valery, and so many others, had cowered in the darkness, afraid to join their eastern brothers for fear of the retribution the Führer would wreak upon the Russian Federation after beating the armies of Russia once more.

The Federation's defeat had never come, however. All across western Russia, similar scenes of ecstasy erupted like blossoms. From the forests of Pskov to the wide plains of Orel, a thousand Valerys leapt to their feet to aid in the reconstruction.

Valery felt his old joints creak as he heaved buckets of wet concrete. He felt his feet drag ever so slightly as he hurried to help. But as he and twelve other Russians pulled on the rope, tearing the swastika down from above Smolensk city hall, he felt the return of emotion long forgotten: pride. The path would belong, and he would surely not live to see it complete, but he knew that one day, Russia would shine brighter than any star in the night sky.

options.name: And the graveyards shall bloom once more.

title: Death from Above
desc:
Anna flew through the skies, enjoying the soft hum of the MIG-27 as it soared through the clouds. Anna loved being up here. It was peaceful. There wasn't anyone in the skies to bother her unlike the chaos on the ground or the roughness of the water. but she wasn't in the skies just for the fun of it today. The war with Germany may have ended, but it seemed the Germans who found themselves in the Russian Federation continue to resist.

"Why do they keep fighting? Can't they see they have lost?" Anna asked herself as she made her descent, flying low as she approached her target.

The Nazi Terrorist group, calling themselves the 'Werewolves' have taken over a farm, killing the owners and turning the place into a fortress. Her job was to bomb the place, lighten the defences up so Ivanov and the boys could clean up the mess. After a few minutes, the farm was finally in sight. She flicked a switch, composing herself as she activated her comms.

"Colonel Ivanov, this is Captain Anna. I'm approaching now. Tell the boys to get their toys ready".

"Copy that, Captain. Ready to move when ready," Dmitri Ivanov replied.

Anna dove down sharply towards the farm, unloading the payload of explosives. She looked over her shoulder as she watched the flames ascend to the skies. The farmhouse and barn were torn to pieces. She sighed as she took to the skies once more. Why are the Germans forcing them to do this? She activated her comms once more, contacting the strike team on the ground.

title: This is Not a Drill
desc:
President Shukshin sat before the radio receiver, sweat dripping from his brow. "I can't believe I'm going to do this," he said. "After all we've fought for, the sacrifices we've made. Has it really come to this?"

Amet-khan Sultan gently placed his hand on his friend's shoulder. "Vasily Makarovich, I understand your trepidation. We all feel fear before any important moment. The anticipation is always worse than the reality. Take a moment and let your nerves settle."

Shukshin nodded, and let his hands rest on the cool pinewood table. Behind them, a clock ticked away the seconds before the plunge. Tick-tock. Tick-tock. A minute passed, then two. Finally, Shukshin picked up the receiver. "Citizens of the Russian Federation," he began, "this is your President speaking. I am forced to address you directly by the severity of the current emergency. The situation in the Moscow region is at a breaking point. The Third Reich has armed rebels and terrorist groups throughout the liberated territory. They are attacking civilians, robbing, raping, looting, destroying all that we've fought to protect."

Shukshin took a breath, wiping the sweat from his brow. "The severity of this emergency cannot be overstated. I have no desire to panic or frighten you, but I must be frank. These ‘Werewolves' are an existential danger to the peace and prosperity of the Moscow region." He took a breath, and steeled himself to change the history of the Russian Federation forever. "As of today," he said, " and with the consent of the Federation Council, I formally declare martial law within the Moscow region."

"This state of affairs will continue until such time as these terrorists have been rooted out and law and order have been restored."

"I assure you," he said, "this is a temporary measure to defeat anti-Russian elements remaining in our territory. This state will not be extended beyond the Moscow region, nor will it be maintained in perpetuity. We simply ask for your trust, and your cooperation, until such time as the emergency has come to an end. We have come to give you freedom- let us work for it together. Thank you."

President Shukshin returned the receiver to its mount with shaking hands. The speech - perhaps the most important broadcast of his life- was over.

"Well done, Vasila," Amet-khan said. "Now we just need to survive the fallout."

"No," Shukshin said. "We need to pray that no tyrant ever uses this precedent to destroy the Federation's democracy."

options.name: Citizens, this is only a temporary solution, please do not shout...

title: Altan Tobchi
desc:
"Gentlemen, thank you for joining me. Please find your briefing packets in the blue folders to your right," said General Georgy Langemak.

The almond-scented boardroom of Feniks Holding Company was filled with businessmen of every kind. Entrepreneurs, managers, and Siloviks sat elbow to elbow at the mahogany conference table- and not all were part of the Feniks team. Yes, there was Aleksandr Belov, CEO of Feniks Infantry Solutions. And yes, there sat Deniska Baladin of Feniks Tractor and Machinery Supply with that stupid smile on his face. But across the table sat Roman Levitsky, COO of Titan Research and Development, and Sergei Novlischev, CGO of Sibir Community Lending. Each of them was just a cog in the machine. But their presence represented something more: an alignment of the megacorporations on the crucial issue of profit.

"If you'll turn to page three, we can begin the executive summary of Fenik Extractive's findings," Langemak said. "Extractive's prospectors presented data indicating significant deposits of gold, uranium, oil, and fluorspar throughout the Mongol countryside. Due to the incompetence of the Kalgan government, and massive resistance from socialist militias and nomad tribesmen, these items are almost universally unexploited."

"I doubt the Mongols will just let us waltz in and take them," Belov said. "Yes, that's correct," Langemak said. "On page eight we've detailed probable long term costs of security operations in the proposed Mongol Republic." Levitsky frowned. "Mongol Republic? I haven't heard anything about this," he said.

"In light of the Federation's orientation away from the Co-Prosperity Sphere, Feniks has devised a strategy to access the Mongol market, and through it a broad East-Asian consumer base," Langemak said. "We intend to take advantage of the instability in the Mengjiang region to empower rebellious liberal elements, as well as restless tribal groups. By arming and supplying the opposition, the Federation will find itself in an optimal negotiating position to obtain favourable trade agreements in a newly born state isolated from its neighbours." "And how do you intend to convince the President and his stooges in the Federation Council?" Levitsky asked. Langemak simply smiled. "The President's a bleeding heart. Have you seen his plans to liberate Armenia, of all places? He hardly needs a push to bring democracy and freedom to an oppressed minority."

options.name: Now, here are the proposed extraction sites...

title: Productive Deliberations
desc:
In the streets of Ulaanbaatar, a car is burning. Dozens of young men, tribesmen and city-dwellers alike, stood beating an iron horse with bats, tire irons, and garbage - anything they could get their hands on. They have lived their entire lives in terrible poverty. Many of their parents were killed in the rebellion. Many more have watched the Japanese and Chinese grow fat on the spoils of the Pan-Asian dream, while their nation, their homes, have grown only fallow. Their rage is spilling over like a tsunami poured into a teacup.

From a window in a nearby office building, Natsagiin Bagabandi watches his peers unleash their anger. He, too, was only a child during the rebellion. His home province of Zhavkhan was burnt to cinders in the endless battles between the People's Revolutionary Council and Demchondongrub's thugs. But unlike his brothers and sisters in the streets, he keeps his anger leashed. It waits by his side, obedient, waiting to be set free.

"The protests are growing," Mendsaikhany Enkhsaikhan said. "I doubt the government will be able to maintain control of Ulaanbaatar much longer."

"I agree. The question is, who will control the city when the Prince's forces withdraw?" Natsagiin said. "The communists in our midst wait in the shadows, but Russia will not be so keen on a red Mongolia." Natsagiin turned from the window to face Mendsaikhany and a dozen Mongolian politicans and a few local entrepreneurs. Each waited, watching him intently, sizing him up. Could this young man be the key to their salvation? Or was he another useless flatterer?

"Mongolia is in crisis," Natsagiin said. "On one hand, despots and cowards that bow to Tokyo. On the other, we the largest force for Mongolian freedom is a relic of a failed ideology. What we need is a third way - something to appeal to the communists and retain the competitive economy and democratic systems that we'll need when we emerge from this mess."

"Our salvation will not lie in conservatism and despotism of all kinds - but that does not mean that socialism is over - it will simply take on a new, collaborative form, assuming we can win it."

options.name: Democracy, good governance, and civil society.

title: Kurultai
desc:
On the banks of the River Tuul, far from cities wreathed in smoke and ash, a blue ger welcomed many, many visitors.

"Hail, brother of the Torghut," said Ganbaatar Batuhan. "Oh, what kind of greeting is that for your old Uncle Batsaikhan?" Ganbat Batsaikhan asked.

"Why, I remember when you were still Little Batuhan, always up to mischief! Come give me a hug!" The old man clutched his nephew with weathered, brown arms and a snaggle tooth smile on his face.

"Oh, but not so young anymore!" Uncle Batsaikhan exclaimed. "With muscles like those, the girls will be crawling all over you!" "Uncle, not now!" Batuhan said with a laugh. "We have to focus on more important things. Here, come inside." Batuhan and Batsaikhan marched into the ger together. Inside, seven weathered, oaken men sat awaiting their host.

"Uncle Batsaikhan, these are our family's guests. Silen-Gioro Ayan, of the Daur. Altangerel Monkhbat, of the Northwest, reaches. Batjargal Timicin, of Kansu. Ganzorig Ulagan, of the Southeast. And Ulagan Baatar, Chuluun, and Esen, his eldest sons." Uncle Batsaikhan merely nodded. "And with myself and Batuhan, we make nine. An auspicious number, Nephew." "We'll need any luck we can get," Ganbaatar Batuhan said.

"I've spoken to each of you by letter. We all know that Demchondongrub's heir is failing. The question is, what will we do? Some in my family have asked me to support the government. Others have asked me to support the Communists. But as head of my father's house, the choice falls to me." The old men nodded as one.

title: All Together, Or Not At All
desc:
"I have been contacted by the Russian President. They want to form a new Mongol Republic, free of communists and dictators alike," Batuhan said. A murmur of dissent bounded from one wall of the ger to another. "Foreigners always seek to exploit us, whether they come from the Middle Kingdom or the North," Ayan said. "I agree," said Timicin. "And they will favour the city dwellers."

"I am with both of you," Batuhan said. "But there are only two sides today: those for the Japanese, and those against. We are all against the Japanese, no?"

"We would not have come if we meant to fight for the Chrysanthemum Throne," Monkhbat said. "I have dealt with the Russians before. A few have a sense of respect."

"I propose this plan. We work together with the city dwellers to force out Japan's dogs. And when the Russians move to establish their puppets, we use our control of the countryside to demand protections for our people," Batuhan said.

"An end to forced relocation?" Ayan said. "At minimum," Batuhan said. "If we fight as the sons of the Oceanic Master, as we all are, then we can demand even more than that."

"And suppose they deny us. Are we going to fight our countrymen? Even if they are city dwellers I have no desire to shed Mongol blood," Timicin said.

"Neither does my nephew," Uncle Batsaikhan said. "But when Chinghiis Khaan united our tribes into the first great Empire, did he not slay Wang Khan and his servants? Surely the servants of Demchondongrub have murdered more Mongolians than the Russians or the Japanese dreamed of. Our responsibility is to our families and our kin. And if that means that we must wield the sword, then so be it."

"Thank you, Uncle," Batuhan said. "That is my position as well. But I don't believe it will come to that. I believe our strength alone will convince the Russians to accept our demands. They will not want to fight a guerilla war against a mobile foe so soon after the war with the Germans."

The seven guests hesitated. But one by one, they stood and offered their support to Ganbaatar Batuhan.

title: NOV_postwar.77.t
desc:
Walking into the empty store, the young man's gaze was drawn away from the cigarettes he had originally intended to buy and instead to the newspaper rack, where the newest newspapers had arrived fresh out of the box. Whistling to himself, he shuffled closer to get a better look.

"[RUS.GetLeader] Sends THOUSANDS of Russians to DIE in Tibetan Mountains - SAVE OUR SONS!" "PRESIDENT SHUKSHIN SUPPORTING MANIACS!" "THE DELUSIONS OF THE PRESIDENT AND WHY YOU SHOULD VOTE FOR THE OPPOSITION!"

The man scoffed, grabbing the paper and scanning the cover page as he paid for his cigarettes. He had known from the very start! [RUS.GetLeader], that slimy bastard, was no angel after all! "Anything else, sir?" the cashier said after the man paid for his cigarettes. "Ah, yeah, actually," the young man replied, setting the newspaper on the counter. "This, please."

"That'll be 15 rubles." the woman stated. Placing his rubles on the counter, he left quickly and settled down on a bench, before taking a cigarette out of the pack he just bought and stuck it in his mouth.

The newspaper took the stance of a concerned mother, deathly afraid that her son would perish in the Tibetan mountains. Russians could not withstand the rough terrain of China, the newspaper wrote, and the lack of consideration for the logistics of an intervention from the Federation would inevitably lead to a catastrophe sooner rather than later. His blood boiled as he stumbled to his feet, clamping the papers shut. The President was making a terrible decision! That was when he realized what he had to do.

This was a democratic country. He didn't have to vote for [RUS.GetRulingParty], and he wouldn't. Next election, he swore, he would do everything in his power to oust the incompetent President out of power. He didn't want to be sent to Tibet to die!

He got up from his chair, tossed his cigarette in the bin, and went to look for another political party to support, grumbling under his breath. Only the ones that could truly represent the youth of Russia would get his vote.

title: The Streets of Krasnodar
desc:
It was another sunny afternoon in the liberated lands of what used to be Kaukasia. General Mikhail Baganov, had decided to spend the day out on the streets amongst the native peoples of the city. As Mikhail wondered, his heart pained upon seeing how the Caucasians interacted with one another. Back home in Russia, the streets were always alive with music and lively conversation. The people of Krasnodar seemed distant from one another. They have isolated themselves as to not draw attention to themselves.

Just how badly had the Germans broken these people? Was the Federation up to the task of bringing hope back to these shattered lands?

Was he?

When the President had personally asked him to lead the new Caucasian administration, Baganov thought he was up to the task. The Federation had managed to pull the largest nation on Earth back together, how hard could rebuilding a smaller region be? After seeing just how broken the lands of formerly German Kaukasia was, he realized just how little he knew about putting things back together.

Caucasia wasn't like Russia. The fields, towns and cities weren't the only things that needed fixing. The people needed healing, spirits had to be mended, social barriers to breakdown and cultures to revitalise. The Germans have ruled for so long, was fixing such a catastrophe?

Baganov shook his head, sighing to himself. Everyone thought uniting Russia was impossible, yet here Russia stood. Everyone thought Germany would easily win again, yet here Russia stood. The aging General looked at the people surrounding him with a look of determination in his eyes. There was no challenge too great for the Federation. He will help these people, no matter what.

options.name: There are no people too broken to help.

title: The Georgian and the Azerbaijani
desc:
In the small Georgian town of Matsimi, once referred to by the Germans as Hessenstadt, there sat two old men on an older porch. They watched workers from all sorts of places rush about. There were Russians and Azeris, Georgians and Adyghe; even a Tatar had passed not too long ago.

"I haven't seen this many people on the streets since the Soviets were pulling outta here!" Giorgi exclaimed to his old friend Yusif. He was visiting from Mahamar, just over the border in Azerbaijan.

"It's strange seeing the Russians so eager to help. I thought those Communists were more eager to subjugate us, like the Germans. It's odd seeing foreigners who care about our people," Yusif said.

"No, no, the Russians are not Communists. Well, not anymore! They're more like Americans now. Fighting for liberty! Battling for democracy! ‘For the liberation of all Russians!" Giorgi said. His powerful emphasis of the Russian President's catchphrase earned a snicker from Yusif.

"Ah, that's right! But we're not Russian, my friend. How do you know we can trust these people? What if they're just softening us up just to smack us down again?" the Azeri asked.

"I'm not so sure, my friend. I suppose we'll just have to trust the Russians this time around. After everything Germany put us through, anything this Federation does will be a million times better than the things the SS did to us," Giorgi said. In the distance, a young girl with freckled cheeks waved the Russian tricolor with a smile on her face.

Yusuf sat back in his chair, thinking on his friend's words.

title: The Black Bear
desc:
"Can you believe we're coming back to the same damn oilfields?" Yusif said.

Huseyn simply shrugged. "My wife needs to eat," he said. "I can't wait for the Federation anymore."

"Too bad reconstruction hasn't gone quicker," Yusif said. "Mohammed told me they hired a couple of guys to rebuild the old grammar school."

"How many?" "Just three." "Damn."

The friends walked together to the admin office of the oil fields. Gravel crunched underfoot, and machinery roared in the distance. The proud flagpole next to the office no longer flew the swastika, and the carved Reichsadler had been torn from its mount above the entryway. But the foundations and the grey stone walls lay unchanged since the day Huseyn first built them at gunpoint.

The pair entered the office and thumped the dirt from their work boots. In the atrium of the building, a young Russian woman sat typing below a banner that read "Welcome, New Employees of Feniks Extractives!"

Huseyn walked up to the desk, and cleared his throat. "Excuse me, miss? My name is Huseyn Abbasov. My friend and I are here to start our first shift."

The young woman turned to the pair and smiled. "Hello! Name Ekaterina Popov. Abbasov, nice to meet. She has employee card?"

Yusif cursed. "She doesn't speak fucking Azerbaijani," he said. "Damn ogras at Feniks sent us an illiterate."

Huseyn just took a breath. "Miss, we can't understand you. Do you speak Turkish?"

She shook her head no.

"Arabic?" Again, no.

He sighed. "Sprichst du Deutsch?"

She smiled and nodded. "Ja, ja! Ich heisse Ekaterina Popov. Womit kann ich Ihnen hilfen?"

title: The Vulture of the Mountains
desc:
Two guards posted at both entry points, all carrying fully automatic rifles. A central command centre is located near the main road, judging from the high security and officers present inside. Two APC's in the parking bay, be mindful of those when entering. There's a bunker door, heavily guarded. That has to be where the rebels are being held.

Dmitri lowered his binoculars, jotting down the observable details on his notepad before rubbing his eyes and wiping the sweat from his brow. He wasn't used to the heat here but he'll manage. The agent sat back against the rocks that lied just behind his perch, settling himself in for the long wait.

The Grey Wolves had taken some Armenian rebels prisoner after ambushing their base of operations. The target of interest was Gurgen Dalibaltajan. He had to sneak into the compound and get the rebels, Gurgen especially, out without being seen by the Turkish troops. Seemed simple enough but unlike the Werewolves, the Grey Wolves were well-armed and well-coordinated. Unlike at home, Russia's Monster didn't have the resources of Russia at his disposal. He will have to be careful if he was to succeed in rebuilding the leadership of the Armenian resistance.

Dmitri sighed, at least he wouldn't be alone in this mission. The rebels had given him a guide to accompany him on the mission, Armen. He was enthusatic to leave the bases. He was the type who liked to explore, according to the other rebels. Staying put didn't do him well.  He would double as a translater since Dmitiri didn't know a lick of Armenian and he is the one was expected to free one of Armenia's best generals. Having a translator would make work here in Armenia much smoother. Speaking of Armen, Dmitri began to wonder just where had his guide run off too?

title: Where it all Began
desc:
When the Federation came to Kazakhstan, the Poles readily accepted the offer of accession to becoming the Autonomous Republic. For the poles of the Republic, many felt that so long as their cultural autonomy was guaranteed, there wasn't much to complain about, especially after the years of anarchy. Then Shukskin started dropping massive amounts of development into the Nowa Polish Republic, and so by the time the Second West Russian War started, the republic served as a model Autonomous Republic. When the Federation went west, The Polish People in Kazakhstan served as the model and dream to convince the various ethnic groups of Eastern Europe to aid in the war against German Oppression.

As the war traveled west, the Polish within the Federation gave everything they could, serving with distinction, after all. Who knew the cost of defeat by the Germans better than the Polish People? When the news reports showed the frontlines getting ever closer to the homeland, the Polish people thought maybe the nightmare would finally end. Finally, when the Federation's army was shown to be right at their ancient homeland's gates, the streets were filled with anticipation and pride. "Maybe," they thought, many hoped to visit their relatives or travel to their old home, and the people of Poland could be rejoined, and another miracle at the Vistula would come.

Then the ceasefire was declared.

Unlike the rest of the Federation and the liberated territories, the Poles of Kazakhstan had relatively quiet celebrations. They understood why it had to be done, but it didn't make the pain of the loss any easier. Nonetheless, the Federation president and the Autonomous Republics' president Stanisław Skalski kept being adamant about eventually freeing Poland from German oppression. So, the Poles of the Federation went back to their daily lives, keeping the story of Poland alive within the Federation, knowing that someday, an opportunity to free their homeland would arise.

Little did they know it would start with the redeployment of the Polish regiments to western Ukraine.

options.name: So long as it is remembered, it can't be truly lost.

title: Poland's Little Green Men
desc:
Kowalski served proudly in one of the Polish Regiments during the Second West Russian war. He didn't care about the values the Federation brought to his town in Kazakhstan, just that they would fight against the Germans. Kowalski remembered being in cities like Volgograd,  Rostov, Kharkiv, Kyiv and ending the war near Brest. Despite the many victories, Poland sitting right across the new border would never sit straight with him. He remained within the Polish units after the war, but his spirit had left, and his passion during the war and prior had disappeared.

When a batch of orders required his unit to move to western Ukraine, he didn't think much of it. Only when his superior decreed they could no longer write letters or make calls about their current location did Kowalski start to question what was going on. When they arrived at the military installation near the Polish border, he was surprised by the raw number of people in rather plain clothing.

Officially, they were polish refugees attempting to flee the violence in the war and were now stuck within the Federation. Unofficially, they were the first batch of proud Poles who were to be trained and equipped to jumpstart the Second Polish Uprising. They were to be equipped and trained, and when the time was right, they would sneak across the border and cause the chaos necessary for the Polish units to cross the border and ‘volunteer' against the German threat.

Kowalski couldn't believe it. Before, it seemed like the Russians only kept the Poles around because they needed everyone against the German threat, but this was different. Poland was to be liberated.

title: Do you Hear the People Sing?
desc:
Helmut's eyes scanned the itinerary, carefully counting every item, only to end with dozens of items missing again.

"We're short, rifles, medical supplies, and grenades. None of them have been checked out, and the last time these supplies were checked on was during the final days of the war."

The man that was his officer, barely a year older than him, let out a tired sigh. "I…. I guess you mark it down as inaccurate. And we'll let the Generals in Konigsberg know when we can reach them, and the communication lines have been spotty for a while now."

"Do….. Do you think the last battalion sold them for rations?"

"No, I don't, Helmut, now start putting what we have in the trucks. We're leaving for Prussia as soon as possible."

While bringing what was the last few old museum piece mausers into the truck, a crowd began to gather. The Poles didn't seem to be making any violent gestures towards them, but their behavior was very different from the last time he was in Poland. For one, their backs stood straight, and their eyes locked with the German Soldiers whenever they bothered to look, and now their eyes, no matter the age, were seemingly filled with passion.

"We don't have time to deal with the untermenschen, driver. Can you drive us out of here?"

The man who sat in the front seat didn't even bother acknowledging rank, he just started to turn on the truck, and the other drivers followed. The trio of trucks roared slowly to start, spurting out toxic and dark fumes, and rolled out of the dusty old warehouse.

As the trucks drove away, Helmut sat opposite of his "officer" and examined his droopy sad patchy black mustache. He eventually mustered the strength to ask why the Poles were behaving the way that they were.

"They're not scared anymore."

options.name: An empire's last breath is typically a whimper.

title: The Raid
desc:
Captain Morozov's specialty had always been counter-insurgency. He had a natural ability for smoking out terrorists, partisans, bandits and everything in between. He had earned his stripes years ago during the Narodnik insurgency, back when the Federation was little more than a city state. When his unit was appointed to deal with a "Werwolf" problem in Moscow, he knew the drill. Many of his superiors objected to his method of trying to find the ring leader instead of breaking up smaller cells, but Morozov believed that cutting off the head of the snake was more efficient than cutting off its tail.

And his methods eventually bore fruit. After a while of listening on wiretaps, collecting info from informants and some "enhanced" interrogation sessions, the Spetsnaz finally located the leader of the Moscow chapter. They tracked the leader to an unassuming house in the outskirts of the city, which belonged to a certain "Boris Ignatyev" also known as "Garmr" to his Werwolf allies. In the middle of the night, Morozov and his men stormed the lonely house, determined to take "Garmr" dead or alive. Unfortunately for them, the house was seemingly deserted, until one of the Spetsnaz discovered a hidden door behind a bookcase. It was hastily opened, and the door opened to a staircase that lead to a secret basement. The unit went down into the basement to discover a makeshift operations room, filled with maps, documents and weapons. The Spetsnaz discovered a man attempting to use the radio to send messages in German, possibly to warn his Werwolf allies that he's been discovered. A voice in Russian yelled at him to stop and turn around slowly with his hands up. Instead of complying, the man tried to pull a gun on the Spetsnaz; and within seconds, "Garmr" was dead.

The Spetsnaz and Russian intelligence agents combed through the documents found and discovered that they've stumbled upon treasure. The man that they killed wasn't named "Garmr" or "Boris" but named "Lutz Hoffmann", an agent of the German Abwehr, tasked with organizing the Moscow chapter of the Werewolves. With the intelligence gathered at Hoffmann's headquarters the Russians found out about every cell, every safehouse,  every supply route, and every planned attack. The next few weeks saw a crackdown of epic proportions. Hundreds of German Werewolves dead and thousands more taken prisoner. They fell like dominoes and the Moscow province was finally free from their terror.

options.name: The end of the Moscow chapter.

title: A People in Healing
desc:
Mere words could never describe the unspeakable horrors that the Caucasian peoples had to endure during Nazi rule. The horrors of life under the Burgundian System, under the iron grip of Josias zu Waldeck und Pyrmont, are unspeakable. Even after his rule ended the damage had already been done, no matter how loose the grip of his successor was. An era of slavery and oppression for the population had left them psychologically scarred. When the All-Russian Army stormed into the Caucuses, they were met with nothing but praise and celebration. After all the suffering and toil, hope has shined brightly over the people as they begin the long journey of finding themselves again.

From the cultural revival programs to simple food and water distribution, the spirit and energy of the population are being revived. The brutalist Nazi architecture is being torn down, and in their place stand memorials for all of those who have fallen during the decade's long occupation. In each city, new apartment complexes are being built, supermarkets are cropping up almost out of the ground- there are even talks of American food chains opening up in Stavropol. The Russian flag flies proudly on the flagpoles of every administrative building in the region, along with their respective flags of the native peoples.

Although these lands are forever scarred by the actions of the Reich, the people have honoured the sacrifices of the Russian people in their efforts to liberate them from tyranny. Across the land, young and old, man and woman, all look towards the shies once more.

options.name: Looking every onwards toward a brighter tomorrow.

title: A New Day in an Old City
desc:
Anton had come a long way from Tomsk, he thought. All this time he marched, and it had finally paid off. There he stood, in the middle of a now nameless street in the once-great city of Minsk, which was reduced to ashes when he and the rest of the army came along. Now, he is stationed there alongside a garrison, at the heart of old Belarus, but also one that was struck the hardest.

The German influence is seen all over, from the architecture to the signs, and especially all the settlers in the area. It made him uneasy, thinking about how horrible the place was before they showed up. Despite this, he'd heard tales from some soldiers stationed in other neighbourhoods; about how a lot of Belarusians didn't enjoy having their houses blown up. But he's just a private, he thought, so Anton didn't worry too much about anything like that happening. He could just direct them to his superiors and watch the shitshow unfold. He cracked a wry grin as the thought passed through his mind.

He passed through the city, essentially off-duty, but still wearing his military fatigues and carrying his rifle. With the reconstruction going on, he must be alert at all times, or so the commanders tell him. Anton thought the city was doing just fine, especially considering how happy the people seemed to be at the Germans being kicked out. As he thought all of this, a scent wafted by him, something warm and impossibly comforting. He immediately followed the scent down the street, checking each corner and alleyway and passing by several soldiers eating the very thing he craved out of massive bowls. His stomach began to rumble; whether or not he was hungry before, he sure was now.

Eventually, he arrived at what initially appeared to be a meager stall, with an old man, probably in his 60's or 70's, and a young woman. Around the stall sat many soldiers, once again eating the same delight Anton had been looking for. Without hesitation, he approached the stall, noting the gargantuan pots and pans with delicious concoctions cooking inside them.

title: Meeting the Ma's
desc:
Several men stood around the refurbished presidential desk that sat in the renovated Kremlin. The table was fairly eccentric, far from the one that the President had used previously, but his advisors swore for days that the table needed to match the new prestige that the President of the Russian Federation held. It didn't need to be this way, but statements backed by action were the quickest way to restore the Russian spirit and power globally. Russia was back on the world stage, and it wasn't going to waste time proving it. As such, it was only natural that one of the first conversations over that desk was what to do with China.

"The Ma's are, as you know, a political faction within Northwestern China; they've held out for decades against Japanese pressure and harbour interest to overthrow the Japanese. Furthermore, they're ideologically varied but not stringent on any particular beliefs. The Ma's are classical Kuomingtang believers, especially the current leader, Ma Jiyuan; ideally, they want democracy and develop China, meaning nothing we would want or suggest to them would be outside of their wheelhouse. In short, they're malleable to our interests and needs, and we can trust they'll be willing to cooperate with us. Especially if we give them enough support that Western China will fall under their rule." When the Chinese Intelligence division department head finished, he looked to the others before finally stopping on the President, waiting to see if the President had any questions to ask.

the president slouching in his chair uttered in an exhausted tone. "Well, obviously, we're going to meet with them, but beyond that, what can we expect?"

"Western China is far from a kind place, and it's unlikely that even united it could overthrow the Sphere. Nonetheless, it can serve as a thorn, and if given the right resources and the right crisis, they could swing eastward and establish their regime. Even if they don't liberate the rest of China anytime soon, having a state between us and the heart of the Sphere that is aligned with us would help us wonderfully. We can build up another market that our businesses can work in, strengthen our image globally, bolster our security, and hopefully make a long-term ally. In short, it's an all-around beneficial idea to help them develop and take over the region, especially if we're planning on a longer-term confrontation with the Sphere."

The president started to fix his sitting position only to utter all the words he needed to, "In that case, then you can get to work with the KMT, send an envoy and start sending supplies along with advisors and support. How long will it take for the Ma's to take all of Western China outside of Japanese rule?"

title: Journey to the East
desc:
Rustam had been traveling over a week with a small contingent of guards and support diplomats when he finally saw the old and faded Kuomingtang in the distance. Beneath the flag, several men with a fair bit dusty but relatively new uniforms stood. Initially, the Chinese soldiers prepared for the worse, aiming their old rifles at the convoy of armored cars. The Chinese lowered their weapons only when Rustam had ordered the soldiers to pull out the Russian flags.

When the Russians finally got to the crossing of Chinese soldiers,  a terse set of glances were exchanged, only to be broken up by Rustam's Mandarian, supposedly the best the Federation had to offer. The Chinese soldiers struggled to follow but understood what the Tartar and the rest of the Russian detail were here for; they were to meet Ma Jiyuan.

The Local Chinese officer offered to take them to Jiyuan personally and joined the Russians on their trip. Rustum used the officer to brush up on the local variant of Mandarin and was taken aback by how nasal the pronunciation of Chinese words were. The two became fast friends, much to the detriment of the driver, who would spend the rest of the trip listening to the two sharing details and information about the Chinese Language. The two didn't even notice when they finally arrived at the center of the Ma Clique.

options.name: The Beauty of language knows no bounds.

title: China's Best Hope
desc:
Rustam tried rubbing off as much dust and wrinkles that had developed over his trip. The second he arrived, he was separated from his new Chinese friend and was taken to what he understood to be a government building. One of the local men asked Rustam to wait a moment in one of the rooms, of which he was happy to oblige; he was beyond tired after the long trip and needed to movement to refocus his mind.

The room itself was a fair bit bland. It had a window, a bed, a table, a few chairs, and a classical Chinese painting on the wall depicting a mountainside. For a moment, Rustam was disappointed, but Rustam was quick to reprimand himself. Only a few years ago did Russia look like this, but despite it, not only did the Federation pull itself up, it stood up to the Germans and came out victories. The Chinese can do the same, especially if given the right push.

A few minutes passed, and finally, a freshly dressed officer appeared outside his doorway and announced that Ma Jiyuan was finally to meet with the Russian envoy. To Rustam's surprise, Ma Jiyuan was far more plane-looking than he expected. He proudly wore his military uniform, with bright and clean Kuomingtang symbols. But the eyes he had betrayed both his sadness and strength. Jiyuan had been fighting longer than most Russians had; it was clear that for him, the war never ended. The first words he heard uttered were not bold promises but an apology.

"I'm sorry for not preparing adequately for your arrival, but we didn't have much clue of when you would be arriving or from what direction; therefore, we haven't prepared food or any of the etiquette fit for a representative of your nation."

Rustam was quick to affirm the general, "Please, you needn't worry. I grew up in a Russia that was being bombed regularly. I understand your position and difficulty perfectly, so you needn't apologize. The one thing I can tell you without a shadow of a doubt is that we understand your struggle, and that is why we're here to help. I'm to become the permanent representative of the Russian Federation to your government. Furthermore, I'm here to inform you numerous supplies and support are to come to assist you and your government in the reclamation of China, starting with the west."

Ma Jiyuan seemingly had weights taken off his shoulders when the admission of aid was uttered. It might have been cold calculus in Moscow or genuine interest in rebuilding China, but for once, in his life; he felt maybe China had a true friend.

title: In the Hall of the Mountain King
desc:
Ali was escorted into the rebel headquarters located deep within the Armenian mountains, beyond the reach of the Turks. He was flanked by two guards, each armed with AV-72's, courtesy of the Federation. At the centre of the room, looking down at a large map of Armenia marked with various crosses and circles, was the head of the Armenian resistance, Gurgen Zanikjan. Ali cleared his throat, getting the Armenians attention. Gurgen looked away from the map, staring the man in the eye for a moment.

"Hello, I'm Gurgen Zanikjan. I'm the de facto head of the resistance. I presume you're with Russian intelligence?" the Armenian asked as he shook Ali's hand. "Ali Gasimov. I'm with the Sluzhba Bezopasnosti" Ali replied, looking him in the eye.

"An Azeribaijani? I must confess, I didn't expect the Russians to send... well, your people to deal with us" Gurgen stated as he took a seat and sat down at the table. The tension in the room was palpable. Despite their isolation, the storm of rivalry that has endured for centuries was seemingly ready to roar at any second. Ali sighed, looking over to the flag of Armenia that hung proudly on the wall.

"Truthfully, Gurgen. I didn't want to be here" Ali began. "When they asked me to come here and negotiate the alliance between Armenia and the Federation, I wanted to say no but..." Ali paused for a moment. He wondered what his ancestors would think of him?

None of that mattered right now. There were bigger things than that. Regardless of what he thought about Armenia, one thing was certain. It did not deserve to be massacred and burned to ash but the Turkish and the insanity that is the Grey Wolves. He may be a son of Azerbaijan, but he refused to stand by and allow this injustice against the Armenians to continue any longer.

"There are bigger things than the rivalry between our two peoples. We have both endured the evils of imperialism. Azerbaijan, thankfully, has been liberated from those who would have sought to annihilate our nation, just as the Turkish wish to do to you. If we want our people to survive these difficult times, we have to put aside our differences and work together" Ali explained, turning away from the flag and looking back at the man in the chair. The room was quiet for a moment before Gurgen slowly began to nod.

"You're right. There are bigger matters than the rivalry between our peoples. I'm willing to set it aside for the sake of freedom. I believe we have business to discuss. Please, take a seat" Gurgen said with a smile, gesturing to the available chair. Ali smiled in return as he took his seat, prepared to get to business.

options.name: Setting aside the past, for a brighter future.

title: Leaving a Mark
desc:
"Where's Baba?" Li Jing asked her mother.

"He left for the factory early this morning, my love," Mama said. "What would you like for breakfast?" They ate porridge and went outside to play.

"Where's Baba?" Li Jing asked.

"He can't come home for lunch, my dear," Mama said. So they ate noodles and talked about the white and black striped butterflies they saw outside.

"Where's Baba?" Li Jing asked.

"He won't be home for a few more hours, my petal. Are you ready for your bath?" Mama said. Jing let Mama wash and braid her hair, but it was no fun without Baba.

"Where's Baba?" Li Jing asked.

"He hasn't finished his shift, little one. Come read with me," Mama said. Of course, Jing knew all the stories by heart. But it wasn't the same without Baba's silly voices.

"Where's Baba?" Li Jing asked.

"He can't tuck you in tonight, my heart. But he left me a kiss to lay on your forehead," Mama said. Jing smiled sadly and laid down to sleep.

At midnight, Li Jing heard the front door close. "Baba, is that you?" she said.

Baba laughed. "Yes it is!" he said. "I missed you, beloved."

"I missed you. Why were you gone so long?" she asked. "Baba has to work, little one," he said. "We need money for rent. But never mind that, look what I got for you!"

He pulled a cloth doll from his pocket. It was the size of a child's hand, made of soft fabric, with buttons for eyes and a tiny scrap of red silk for a heart.

Li Jing took the doll and smiled. "I love it, Baba! Thank you!"

Her father knelt and kissed her on the cheek. "I love you, my daughter."

options.name: To understand your parent's love, you must give it to others.

title: Forget Me No Longer
desc:
The Mauser rested softly in the crook of Davit's shoulder, with its stock nestled into the dark dirt of Dilijan. The night sky above cloaked the landscape in darkness, and the fire crackled softly, its tempo erratic. In his hands, a relic of the past. It was another night, for Davit... if that was something to find pride in, now. His hands, calloused and scarred, gripped firmly along the edge of the photo. Its dusty, black-and-white colouration was illuminated by the flickering flame in front of him, with the smudged little figures only slightly visible.

His eyes quietly drifted along the front, eyes looking upon those grainy little figures. He'd seen this sight perhaps a thousand times over, now- had sat aside this campfire over and over again, after days worth of fighting. His thumb, running softly along the side of the photo, ever slightly ruffled its dirty white edges. He could still remember their voices, occasionally. Could remember their smiles- their laughter, even in the face of their circumstances before. Their youth..that which was stolen from them. Perhaps, back then they'd have been here, sitting by his side. Perhaps, he wouldn't have had to be the only one left- perhaps there could've been some hope, for the future of their people. They'd called themselves Fedayi for a reason- 'those who sacrifice'. That was not the case, for him.

Anoush, Tigran, Arax..all gone, now.

He'd fought for so long, now..since he was a young boy. He'd fought for Armenia, yet- he had yet to die for Armenia. He'd lost his friends, his family...he'd lost what made it anything to him. His teeth, under the scraggly beard that adorned his face, were tightly grit. The feelings within him, he could not describe- a concoction of rage and hurt. Was this his fate? To fight forever, for the sake of a people that he could never feel the joys of?

He would either die or be alone. Either meet his end, or, by some means- kill, and kill, and kill, until he finally stood alone, atop a mountain of corpses with which nobody else to finally appreciate the view. What could be won here? Would it ever be worth it?

Davits face, pampered with dust and soot, had been disturbed by the solemn flow of red-hot tears. There was no means of controlling it, anymore- nothing to hold him back. He missed them, he missed his family-he damned every god possible and damned the Turk. None of it would soothe his pain, and none of it would end this cycle.

Under that night sky, that son of Armenia sobbed...

options.name: knowing he could not appreciate the fruits of his own struggle.

title: The Future of Armenia
desc: With the Mountain War having come to a close, debate has broken out within the Federation and Presidential Office as to what will become of newly liberated Armenia. Many, most of all the people of Armenia themselves, have called for the region to retain its status as an independent nation, while some call for its integration into the greater whole of the Federation as an Autonomous Republic. Whatever the President decides, the future of Armenia rests in his hands.

options.name: Integrate Armenia into the Caucasian Federation.
Annex Armenia as an Autonomous Republic within the Federation.
Armenia has been subjugated for too long. They shall remain independent.

title: Blue Lakes, Red Grass
desc:
The halls of the Assembly jolted to life as Shukshin stepped forward into Ahmet-Khan's office, trailed by an entourage of foreign correspondents and regional administrators. With each official clutching stacks of papers to their chest, the hustle and bustle of their movements was almost mesmerizing to a passerby, but as the President confidently strolled into the Minister's Office, the demeanor of the room stood in stark contrast to the madness outside the doors.

"Vasiliy, how are you? We have some, pressing matters to discuss." Ahmet-Khan's tone seemed to calm the tension within the cramped interior, yet his eyes were focused solely on Shukshin's ever-colder gaze. taking a seat before the Foreign Minister, Ahmet opened a small vanilla folder before the President, presenting the intelligence dossier before him.

"Hungary has fallen into civil war since the fall of the Reich. Hungarian Nazis have seized the capital of Budapest, leading to a short but swift disintegration of all formal administration in the region."

The President slowly scanned the contents of the document, his racing mind attempting to formulate a solution for the troubling situation.

"The Hungarian Red Army has taken advantage of the present power vacuum, while a democratic coalition of Agrarians has reached out to our intelligence agency, pleading for our assistance. Recent photographs taken by reconnaissance aircraft show an increasing buildup of German soldiers on the Hungarian border. While the Reich seems to be descending into internal chaos, it appears that a Nazi foreign intervention is not out the question, Mr. President."

Sinking into his chair, Shukshin let out a pained sigh, sliding the document back towards his longtime friend. "The Germans are weak, our recent victory has proved that. While a direct relief force is out of the question given the volatile nature of the decrepit Reich, we cannot idle by while the Fascists grow in number. If the DSPR want to offload our surplus, fine! We will send it to Hungary. Get yourself a phone call with the leader of these 'Agrarians' of yours, and make their dreams come true."

options.name: 'If that's what you wish, Mr. President.'

title: A Black Siberia
desc:
Where there was loyalty to the League's principals, there was always treachery, and the Captain always had a nose for treachery. Dancing from corner to corner, the penned executioner finally found his next target for “questioning”. Standing idly by next to the ill-appropriate light afforded by the rusted lamppost, reading his paper in the company of none.

“Comrade citizen,” he bellowed out to the younger man. “Would you lend me a minute of your time?”

“O-Oh, uh, Comrade" the Man began. “I r-really should be off to work. Got lost in the pages as they say, right?”

“Nonsense!” Captain Dyatlov waved his gloved hand. "I insist.."

Slowly the Captain approached, placing his cuff on the young man's shoulder. Dyatlov let a grin creep upon his face, the fear was palpable.

“What’s your name, Comrade?”

“It’s V-Viktor, Viktor Semyonov."

"Well then, Viktor! You are glad I came across you. I.. consider myself more lenient than others. We can talk for a bit, maybe chat about this fine paper in your possession."

“S-Sir, I'm a-afraid if I don't get going soon, the Store's going to ope-"

"Say Semyonov, where do you work? I don't blame you for taking your time. Can't see much in this fog, you can get lost without keeping track." the Captain bored his gaze into the young man's frightened eyes, directing them to the pavement below.

"A-Anastasia's Books, just off Molokova Street."

"Is that so? And what kind of books do you sell at such an establishment?"

"U-Uh, well, I guess all kinds. Childrens, History, Philosophy. We sell whatever w-we can find, really. I work the counter and the children seem to l-love it."

Dyatlov paused for a moment, letting his artificial grin slowly turn into a face of stone.

“Well, off you go, Viktor Semyonov. I hope your work finds you well in your future endeavors."n
"O-Of course, Sir. Glory to Russia!" the man quickly scurried off into the boundless smog, leaving the Captain alone in the light.

Dyatlov reached his glove into his breast pocket, removing a small black booklet from its confines. He flipped past hundreds of identical columns before stopping on a single blank box.

options.name: Suspect 51: Viktor Semyonov. Suspected of spreading subversive literature to palatable youth. Appropriate Action: Immediate Disposal.

title: An Atmosphere Of Silence
desc:
Maxim had sat at his desk rhythmically assembling the slides of the several rifles he was ordered to make. For the past week he had been biting his tongue, the quota had been extended and now he worked through the night. He had already been making the allotted amount of weapons parts, hell he even made more most days.

“Tima what is this shit, we’ve been making the parts and now they do this to us?”

Tima quickly muttered, “Maks stop this, don’t you remember Vitya, do you want to get shot?”

Before Maxim could respond Tima walked away to ‘get parts’. Annoyed, Maxim went back to assembling slides, hearing the crunch of a League soldier on the catwalk. In fear, he quickly returned to making slides, his adrenaline-riddled hands forming several slides at once.

Before long, Tima came back and glared at his weapon parts muttering a few comprehensible words under his breath. Before long the loudspeaker croaked its awful song, “Factory Worker 4673 enter the nearest office, Worker 4673.” Inevitably the speaker stopped and quietly beset the factory. What used to be the eyes of his coworkers, whom he’d share occasional small talk with turned into dark coals. The Factory had gone silent as the ringing in his ears prevailed and he stood up, his legs aching after each stride.

The door to the office was heavy, groaning as he pushed it open. Inside this simple room stood two Black League soldiers and an officer, who welcomed him in. After sitting in silence for what felt like hours the officer finally spoke,

“What is your name worker?”

Maxim cleared his throat and muttered,

“Maxim Larionovich sir, but my friends call me Maks.”

“So you make the slides of rifles Maxim?”, the officer retorted back. Before he answered Maxim noticed a glint in the officer's eyes, a degree of morbid sadism spreading to his lips.

“Yes sir, I make the slides primarily of rifles but I can also make other weapons parts.” Maxim had replied.

In a few swift swipes, the officer crossed multiple boxes on a document, before staring at Maxim.

“Thank you for your cooperation Worker 4673.” The officer then grabbed his pistol and waved goodbye to Maxim, pulling the trigger.

options.name: They shall not corrupt our works...

title: Teach Them Hate
desc:
Ivano sat in his classroom although the last time he did so was many many years ago. There was no sweet teacher who taught everyone with a grace about basic topics such as Russian, Mathematics, and the small world around them. It was replaced with a grizzled and aged man, his face bearing a large scar down towards the tip of his nose and nearing his eye a glass one replaced what once was his own.

After sitting down the teacher introduced himself as Lazar and pulling down a clean map had shown all of Russian territory they had and with some additions, pointing westwards Lazar explained that Russia had been raped and pillaged by the Germans so much that even some of the Russian people had began to join the rank and file of the German army. 

Hearing this, and well seeing this horrified Ivano. He had heard stories from the west of some of the atrocities occurring in Western Russia. But if what he heard was true then what else had the Germans done?

Lazar, aware he shook the throng of civilians, continued to list depressing statistic after depressing statistic almost demoralizing them to the point of depression. Before ending he decided to give the people something to hate.

“What is it we can do?” one woman exclaimed.

“You can work harder, longer, and help us fight the teutonic menace with all the patriotic zeal you can muster!” Lazar responded.

title: A Slight Divergence
desc:
Yekaterina was in the middle of her work. She was checking papers in the central bureau where the most important documents about everything from military operations to propaganda campaigns to rally the population. All of that she had been entrusted to take care of. It was quite surprising considering her gender, and in spite of both dangerously low wages and the misogyny she experienced, she liked her job.

As she searches through the files detailing political prisoners, it seems that there are files that detail the location of political prisoners are missing. She checks multiple times before concluding that it is unnecessary. There had been multiple times before that documents were organized improperly, however that was just for pretty simple ones, these ones were in one of the deepest parts of the bureau. It was a discrepancy she never before had seen, while she wasn’t that worried, it still was strange.

She rose and walked to her office table where she wrote down that five files had disappeared. Right as she wrote it down she started to contemplate if it really was a good idea to note it down or not. When there had been a rare inconsistency before, she had always been yelled at by the boss, even if it was never her fault. Her male colleagues were only occasionally yelled at by the boss, even if it was the exact same discrepancy found. She continued to write, she slowly became more and more nervous. Finally she erased it. It was no big deal, right. As she slowly took a deep sigh of relief, she walked back to her work, continuing with searching through the files.

title: Some Never Grow Old
desc:
The Family Petrova may have been an ordinary family in the Soviet Union, this is however not the case after the Great Patriotic War and the arrival of the Black League. The family was split up after the Great Patriotic War and now can rarely send letters, only through secret contacts through Kazakhstan can they get their letters to Muscovy.

Elyna Petrova was doing her usual business taking care of the house. She couldn’t take her mind off the letter she got four months ago. Her husband trapped in Muscovy had gotten a job as a soldier in the Moskowien Wehrmacht and he would soon be able to reunite with her. She sent a reply immediately as she explained her concern about the Black League discovering her ties with a collaborator. Usually a response would take about four to six weeks. She hadn’t gotten a response in five months. She had grown to be strong, even after being driven away from her husband. In the early days she would cry herself to sleep every night. Now she was ready to fight against anything coming in her way, including the rigid Black League.

The doorbell rang, it rang across the small apartment. Someone coming to their house was something very unusual. She quickly walked towards the front door. She opened the door to see five policemen, all with uniforms black as the night. The head officer started speaking.

“Mrs Petrova, I am afraid we are going to have to arrest you for subversive actions against the All-Russian Black League and for having contacts with Collaborators.”

“WHAT!?! YOU CAN’T-”

The Officers proceeded to turn the apartment upside down and arrested the rest of her family left in Russia, her Mother, Father and son... They were put into the trucks of the officers. They were driven away and forgotten to history.

options.name: Another family removed so that the Great Trial can prevail.

title: The Gears Grind On
desc:
As all Black League personnel are subject to the highest standards of fitness, Glakoverkh Yazov was ordered on this date by BLP-DR-078431 (AMOSOV, Nikolai Mikhailovich) to desist from his duties and report for a complete physical and mental examination. During this period, leadership of the Black League was devolved from Yazov to Evgeniy Savintsev; duties of the Glakoverkh were divided between the leadership cadres as outlined in Succession Document 178.

Evgeniy Savintsev began the day as he did every other, with a steaming cup of black coffee and two hundred push ups. From 06:30 to 09:30, he reviewed the names of five hundred criminals, dissidents, and malformed individuals sentenced to the Redemptionary Brigades. He assigned two hundred and thirty seven to rebuild the highway between Irkutsk and Krasnoyarsk, and one hundred and twelve to mine clearing duties on the Moscowien-Russian border. The remainder were shipped to Vorkuta, to assist in Black League training operations. At 10:15, he left his desk for a three mile run with Foreign Minister Aleksandr Sakharovsky, wherein they agreed to conduct an assassination of several pro-democracy advocates in Romania.

At 11:45, Aleksandr Sakharovsky met with several members of the “Foreign Ministry'', to discuss the issue of Turkmenistan. Central Asia, as the borderlands of the Russian National Reclamation Government, occupied an increasingly large place in Sakharovsky’s mind; it is a place of dissent, of weakness, of degeneracy and anti-Black League thinking, infested by Bolsheviks and fascists alike. Eventually, a junior member of the cadre offered a suggestion that caught Aleksandr’s eye: a mass resettlement of vetted, loyal Russian populations into the largest cities of Central Asia, and a temporary displacement of unvetted Turkish and Khazak populations from the region.

At 14:20, Sakharovsky gathered with Evgeny Pitovranov and the leadership of the Economic Ministry to discuss ongoing preparations for the Great Trial. Pitovranov has repeatedly requested additional labor resources to complete fortifications on the Nowa Polska-Moscowien border, but has been rebuffed several times by both Yazov and Savintsev. Together, Sakharovsky and Pitovranov draft a proposal to mobilize the Redemptionary Brigades in low priority industries,  freeing trustworthy laborers to shift to building forts, pillboxes, and life saving defenses.

At 18:00, Pitovranov and Yuri Drozdov spoke over dinner concerning a wave of sabotages in Central Siberia. Drozdov suspects remnants of the Siberian Black Army; Pitovranov surmises the presence of German agents. They agree only that security must be doubled. Together, they compose a plan to make Novosibirsk a closed city, expelling all women, children, and unvetted civilians and permitting only trustworthy laborers to stay. Soon, this plan will extend to all major industrial hubs throughout the Reclamation Government. The traitors and the saboteurs will have nowhere to hide.

At 24:00, Glakoverkh Yazov returned from the examinations. His desk was empty, for once. He marched to his chambers, removed his shoes, and slept without worry.

options.name: Leadership entails creating new leaders, not followers.

title: The Costs Of Victory
desc:
The unification of Russia had brought something into Dimitry Yazovs life that he’d only fakely expressed to his subordinates. For once, he could now truly say without a doubt that he now possessed a sense of certainty. He could now be fully confident in the Leagues strength, and he would now truly be at the helm of his peoples destiny. But, there were issues at hand that needed to be taken care of. After all, he couldn’t simply run head first into the lands of the Aryan.

The assembly assembled before him had been assigned to hammer out a solution to every problem the League is facing or could face in the coming months. Lasting long into the night, it became clear that there were indeed several issues that had to be resolved, lest the League's chance for success in the coming Trial be at risk.

The most discussed topics included the problem of production capability, access to resources, and technological advantages that their enemy held. There were ways to solve such issues of course, but it became clear to the assembly that implementation of reforms would be severely hampered by the current economic capability of the League.

Yazov felt a burning sensation in the back of his head upon hearing those last words, and stood up to speak, immediately silencing everyone present.

“I think you’re all forgetting a core part of what made our state triumphant in unifying the Motherland. When we marched onward to reunify Russia, we did not do so only because we had such things as advantages in production capability or overwhelming firepower.”

All eyes were on Yazov now, as each man began to squirm uncomfortably in their seats.

“We triumphed because of our will, and unwillingness to ever give up on our peoples right to see the day when vengeance could be achieved in full. Yet you sit here and tell me that our will is no longer enough to solve the current issues at hand?”

options.name: “We will immediately move to implementation, sir.”

title: Name, Age, And Place Of Birth
desc:
“Next.”

Checkpoint officer Vasily Smirnov rubbed his temples with his thumbs while the next feckless idiot shuffled up to the booth.

“Name, age and place of birth.”

“Well, uh, it’s Ivanov,” the small, beetle-shaped man mumbled, “Ivan Ivanovich, that is.”

“You taking the piss?”

“Of course not, comrade checkpoint officer.”

“Hand over your papers,” Smirnov groaned, “I trust you have them on you.”

Ivan Ivanov winced as he passed a single passport beneath the glass. Smirnov sighed when he saw the hammer and sickle on the front cover.

“This look like the Soviet Union to you, Ivanov?”

“Well, its the most current—

“Most current?” Smirnov laughed, “Trust me, Ivanov, if you want to fool somebody, don’t act so fucking daft.”

“It says here, comrade sir, I was born in Sverdlovsk.”

“You don’t expect me to read this shit, do you Ivanov? Are you delusional?”

For a moment, Ivanov looked ready to burst into tears as he shuffled nervously. Just as Smirnov thought he was about to walk away, he spoke again.

“That lady that just passed through, she’s—

“Your wife? I’ve heard it all before Ivanov. I don’t give a fuck if its true or not, it comes down to this: if you can’t show me anything printed this decade, you’re not getting in. Understand?”

“Well, I have this.”

Smirnov felt his hairs stand up and his smile drop as Ivanov passed through a crisp slip of paper with a black swastika stamped on top. He examined it for a moment before speaking again.

“Ivan Ivanovich, you are a citizen of the German Reich?”

“Moskowien, to be precise, but yes.”

“And why are you attempting to enter Russia?”

“To escape,” Ivanov stared at him blankly, as if it were obvious, “to reunite with my family.”

“Ivan Ivanovich, are you aware that this document is tantamount to treason against Russia, and undeniable proof of collaboration with the German occupiers?”

“Treason?” Ivanov paled, “That can’t be true. I’ve never collaborated. How could I have?”

“Well, Ivan Ivanovich,” Smirnov reached over to the telephone, “That’s for us to find out.”

Smirnov put the telephone to his ears and waited for the tone. When he heard the grunt of the man on the other end, he spoke.

“Yes, this is Smirnov at point D, I’m gonna need a hand or two. No, nothing dangerous, just a collaborator. Oh, and his wife may have gotten through, one, uh, Maria Ivanova. I’d advise liquidation upon sight. She’s not likely to know anything.”

title: For all to see
desc:
Was it a dream? Elias wasn’t sure what had just happened. Ever since the Russians had come and thrown everyone into the old ghettoes, hunger had gnawed at his stomach without end. Some of the other kids had taught Elias to drink as much water as he could, to trick his stomach into being full. Elias thought it worked, but deep down he knew that in the end it was only a trick. The grown-ups knew it too, and so they sent the children out every morning to beg the guards for some food. Usually, the guards would just scream and kick at them until they ran away. But today, when nobody was looking, the old man with the kind eyes had leaned down and reached through the barbed wire and passed Elias a backpack, filled with bread.

Elias hurtled down the streets of the ghetto with the bag strapped to his back. He felt the eyes of starving Germans and Russian guards on him as he bolted, but he wouldn’t stop until he made it home. With every step, the bag seemed to become heavier and heavier, like it was filled with bricks. Even when it was so heavy that he felt like his back was on fire, Elias refused to slow down. His house was just around the corner.

When he burst into his home, he saw Papa and Opa, but they were not alone. About twelve other men were crowded around the kitchen table, studying a map that was spread across the surface. Red arrows and crosses had been drawn all over it, and Elias thought he even saw some rifles in the corner of the room. Before he could understand what was happening, he collapsed from the effort he had just spent. As Papa rushed over to him, a few of the other men cheered to see the bread overflowing from his bag. Elias smiled weakly as they sung and danced and Papa ran his hand over his head.

In an instant, the world turned white. Elias tried to ask what was happening, but his mouth was empty and his ears were full. When he tried to scream, his mouth filled with ash and blood. He didn’t have long to think, before a force stronger than anything he could imagine pressed down on his chest. Just as quickly, the fabric of the world seemed to rip, and a sea of blackness came rushing through the gaping chasm.

When the smoke had cleared and the ash had settled, a messaged had been scrawled across the ruined building in hateful black paint.

options.name: Know your fate. Resistance is hopeless.

title: We Are Ready
desc:
The door slammed shut, and silence returned to the bunker that served as Dmitiry Yazov’s quarters. Yazov and his staff had concluded yet another meeting, with the main talking points being on the current status of readiness for the Leagues troops and reports on the morale of the people. Dozens of files containing dizzying amounts of data had been laid out on the table before him, and Yazov had slowly combed through each and every one. When the meeting concluded, his outward persona completely changed, going from the cold, iron hearted man that the world knew, to a man shakily taking off his cap and taking several swigs of vodka.

So much work had been done. So many production facilities were created, dissidents crushed, military units trained and organized, and so much more that Yazov had begun to start wishing that the day would come sooner. The day when he would give that order, and it could begin. The day the Motherland’s redemption would finally be achieved when The Great Trial was commenced. But at the advice of his staff, he’d delayed that order so that Russia could well and truly be prepared for The Great Trial.

And now, after so long, that day was on the horizon. Finally, he thought. Finally, it would all be worth it. Every moment of progress, gained in blood since the day his mentor had given him the mantle of leading the Leagues destiny, would all be worth it. When the day came where Russian flags flew over Germania, and the Aryan was obliterated by Russian arms... finally, justice for innumerable crimes against his people would be achieved at last.

Yazov sighed, rising from his seat and reaching for his hat as he remembered once more that there were still a few remaining tasks at hand that needed to be addressed before all of his thoughts could come to fruition. He exited his room, and made his way over to the broadcasting station as he prepared himself for one last grand speech to his people before destiny.

title: All for One
desc:
Just days ago, Yegor was supposed to be fighting Teutons. Instead he busied himself with hoofing it the other direction, opposite the frontline, in the dead of night, with some extra supplies he “borrowed” for his journey. Deserting didn’t mean anything to him. He was an only child, and the only one taking care of his parents when they got grey and old. He couldn’t stand to think of how they were just barely surviving without him so he ran. He had considered the thought they might come for his family after he deserted, so he needed to just get home and get them the hell out of Russia.

Finally, he saw his village on the horizon, standing atop the hill as it always has. Yet, with all the men conscripted and gone, it seemed dead and grim. He rushed up the hill, past the market, and all the way down to the other edge of the village; the only people around to observe him were elderly women and the youngest of children.

He entered the home where he grew up and took a few more steps, into the old familiar living room, finding his mother sitting on the couch, staring ahead with eyes dead and energy completely depleted. She looked almost 10 years older, and didn’t even acknowledge Yegor as he came in.

“Mother, you’re here! We need to go, I need to get you and father out of here. Where is he? I’ll go fetch him while you pack-”

“They took him.” She replied, without a trace of emotion in her voice. She would have cried, had she any tears left.

“B-because of me...?” Yegor asked, dread running throughout his nerves.

“No. They just needed him. Gave him a uniform, a gun, everything. Told him he’s going west.” She said, finally daring to look her son in the eyes.

Yegor’s heart sank. These monsters didn’t even care that he had deserted, they just needed everyone, even an elderly man at the end of his life. He knew the conditions out there, on the front; it is no place for old men.

Yegor sat down next to his mother as he wrapped his arms around her and held her close, both of them staring into nothingness as thoughts better left unvoiced ran through their heads.

title: The Truth in the Numbers
desc:
Abrasha sat in a dark room, with the cold embrace of his metal chair and table being the only outside stimuli to keep him from outright sleeping right then and there. Today, he’d been ordered to come in and work on “A new set of data” for him to process and organize. Truth be told, he would take anything new as a blessing.

He’d spent months chipping away at the same old administrative paperwork, after having been reassigned from his beloved home of Tomsk to the depressing and minimalistic city that the League called a capital. Despite the food rationing and lack of anything resembling goods for a middle class, Abrasha’s main issue was simply boredom.

But now perhaps Abrasha could get something new. Maybe it would even put the skills he’d gained in university to use. And as he read through and examined each folder given to him, he displayed a barely noticeable smile. His wish had come true, and he tried to savor the moment as much as he possibly could in times where happiness could be considered its own luxury.
