Auguste felt a small drop of water hit his cap, and then another and another. The tide was coming in. Sitting down on a street corner beside a child-sized shadow, he pulled his pistol from its holster. France was gone. He was an echo of a bygone era. There could be no resistance without France.

He never would see Paris.

title: RAD_EU.47.t
desc:
The low roaring wail of the air sirens colored the air, as in so many drills past. Although, this would be unlike any drill Heinrich had ever been in. His small classroom of secondary school children clamored beneath their desks, the howl of the raid sirens doubly increasing the anxiety of the affair. He clutched at his journal as a child half his age might, gripped with authentic fear. Cowering beneath his desk, he could do little but wait.

Remembering the training of the Jugend, he began to breathe, something he had forgotten before. It would all be over soon; the all clear would be called, and it would turn out to be a surprise drill.

Inhale, count to four.

Beneath his desk, Heinrich turned to Herr Meyer, his Party Ethics teacher. The old man was nowhere to be seen. Only a blank chalkboard stood in his stead. Suddenly, Heinrich heard one of the children yell, "Herr Meyer is cowering behind his desk!" Exhale, count to four.

Some children sniggered. Others began to weep. Inhale, count to four.

In the distance, through the thin glass pane of the room's single window, streaks of orange, white and red blazed through the afternoon sky over the city. Heinrich thought they looked like the jet planes he saw in parades. These jets were not in the eloquent formations Heinrich was familiar with, however. They were scattered, and converging on a distant point. Exhale, count to four.

Heinrich did not need to wait long to find their skyborne quarry. Rather, their quarry found him. A single black dot in the far, far distance ignited in a flare of awesome white light. In an instant, a second Sun was born on Earth, and it's blinding baptismal flame darkened Heinrich's vision into nothing. Inhale, count to four.

The now blind Heinrich could only hear the screams of his classmates, and the wail of the sirens. This was not a drill. This was real.

title: RAD_EU.37.t
desc:
Men frantically emerge from their barracks, in a dash to their emergency stations. Sirens blare a deafening tone throughout the reserve army compound. Theodor emerges from the garage in the midst of the commotion, confused and dazed. The panic seems uncharacteristic of the usual action drills that have become common since his units readiness status was upgraded.

Noticing one of his officers jogging by, he takes the opportunity to learn of the chaos. "Sir, what's the panic? Another drill?" Theodor asks loudly. The officer halts his stride and turns to face Theodor, his face flushed, as if all the worries of the world are upon his shoulders. "There's no drill. Run to the armoury, Feldwebel. The bombs have been launched." the officer retorts.

Theodor feels his heart sink inside his chest, and feels as if he is going to puke. Instead of following his orders to report to the armoury, he doubles back and retreats to his garage. Frantically, he begins work on preparing the truck he was working upon to drive. He swiftly places all removed parts back to their respective spots and secures them. Slamming the hood back down, he notices two of his subordinates returning with their rifles.

Attempting to avoid his men, Theodor does not acknowledge their presence, and begins to climb into the cabin of his truck. "Feldwebel, where are you going? Where's your rifle?" asks one of his men. Continuing to ignore them, he turns the key. Much to his relief, the engine roars to life with little delay. "What are you doing?" exclaims his subordinate. "Leaving." replies Theodor, as he begins to slowly reverse the truck out through the garage doors. Of a sudden, a deafening gunshot rings out, and he feels winded. He struggles to retain his breath, as another gunshot rings out. In a panic, he clumsily falls from the cabin. His subordinates stand above him, shell casings upon the floor.

title: RAD_EU.28.t
desc:
He was not sure how long he had been beneath the earth. Weeks? Months? Did it even matter? When they arrived, they were promised utopia, safety, the opportunity to remake the world in their image. But the promises fell apart the moment he stepped off the train. The vault doors were improperly sealed, so they had to dynamite the tunnel outside to protect everyone from the fallout. Half the food wasn't delivered, and none of the physicians had arrived, so famine and disease ran rampant. The provisions turned moldy, the water turned black, the very walls began to rust. Roofs caved in, and the upper levels were uninhabitable. Everyone had dropped dead around him like flies, touched by the finger of God - or the hand of the Devil, whichever was closer.

And now he was all alone, sobbing in the darkness. The power had run out a while ago, and the heating a little before that. He had briefly resolved to survive by drinking the putrid water that dripped from the ceilings, but food became an issue, and he could not resolve himself to eat the corpses of his friends and family. So he lay in the dark, waiting for the end. Would it be suffocation? A gas leak? Starvation? Dehydration? Hypothermia? Or would he despair so much that he simply resolved to stop living?

Soon, he got his answer. A loud thud, deep and distant. Then another, and another, a successive chain of thuds, now joined by the cries of bending steel and the tumbling of rocks. A cave-in. He didn't run or try to flee - he simply lay on the cold, slimy floor and hoped that the collapse would crush his head first.

title: RAD_EU.24.t
desc:
She woke with a start, breathing shallow breaths. She couldn't see, she couldn't move; all she could smell was smoke. With no small effort, she wrenched herself free, crawling towards a pinprick of light. Her breathing was heavy now. She had been beaten by the handlers the night before for not working fast enough. When they had dumped her in the quarters, she had heard a thunderous roar, as if a thousand thousand gunshots had fired into her ear. She didn't remember anything else.

As she approached the light, frantically moving rocks and chunks of concrete out of the way, she became aware of a dull pain in her gut. She rolled onto her back, and felt for the source of the pain. As her hands clasped around the large chunk of wood embedded in her stomach, her eyes filled with tears as the pain hit in full force. She had to get out. She had to escape.

Swallowing her sobs, she crawled once more towards the light, hands bloody and raw as she scraped them against the stones. The light slowly, gradually, grew bigger and bigger, until she could just barely crawl through into the world beyond.

She had never been so grateful to see the sky, and as she slowly, unsteadily, rose to her feet, she couldn't help but smile at the ashes and the ruins of what had once been a slave camp. She grinned ruefully at the body of a nearby German--he had always been the kindest to her, but in these camps that meant he was only slightly gentler with his beatings. She laughed, some blood spurting from her mouth as she made her way to the edge of the camp, staring at the sky.

She was dying, she knew that. She had sat by her mother's side on the day she breathed her last, and now she had a feeling she'd breathe her own last breath soon. As she sank down, she still found herself smiling. For, unlike her mother, and her mother before her, she would die a free woman. No more Germans here, she thought, bitterly.

And as the life left her eyes, she whispered a thanks to the God that had abandoned her people for so long.

title: RAD_EU.18.t
desc:
The world was in chaos. Men sprinted for whatever cover could be found. Cars, buildings, the underground. One woman even lifted a manhole and headed for the sewers. For Beatrice, time stood still. Only the faintest echo of what had till a moment ago been a normal Sunday afternoon in Piccadilly registered in her mind. As the alarm blared overhead, she found herself incapable of thought, until a gentle tug at her left hand brought her back to the terrible reality.

"Mummy, what's happening?" asked Simon, her youngest.

The deepest agony any mother could ever feel racked Beatrice to her core. Her own fate, she could accept, but for little Simon and his big sister Lisa - herself holding Beatrice's other hand - the thought was too terrible to bear. She had visions of them both burning in the flames of Inferno come to Earth, and her mind immediately rushed to where they too might find shelter.

But she knew that they were right in the heart of the capital, and in spite of the efforts of the panicking crowds around them there would be very little to be achieved by hiding. Images filled her mind of what might happen if they did live. Of Simon succumbing over many weeks to the ravages of radiation. Of Lisa wasting away in a world where all the food had turned to ash. Of them both having to watch as she was dragged away by maddened survivors in search of a slave. Or food. Or worse.

The world might turn right again, one day. But she knew none of them would live or remain sane long enough to see it. So she did the only thing she could do. She sat down on the steps of the old theater and held her children tight, like she did every night before bed. Through her tears, she told them of how much they made her proud, of how much she loved them every day, and how she knew that they would stay together, wherever they were going.

"Where are we going, mummy?" asked Lisa through shuddering sobs. In the sky above, a tiny shape began to make its final descent.

"To heaven" said Beatrice.

Then there was a flash. And all that was left was a dark shadow on the steps.

title: RAD_EU.15.t
desc:
The Obergruppenführer watched the throngs of people massing outside of the compound, desperately trying to clamber over the fence and past the guards. He could almost hear their cries - "Let us in!" "Don't leave us to die!" "We're German, like you!" - German, yes, but not German enough. Neither was he, which was why he was here and not in a bunker hundreds of kilometers away. A steep cost, sure, but an acceptable one for an Aryan utopia.

All that was left were a few documents to sign - formalities, really - and a few goodbye calls to make before joining his family. His wife had already taken the liberty of giving the pills to the children, all of them brave to the last. In a few minutes, he would-

"They didn't arrive!" the aide yelled with panic as he burst into the room.

"What didn't arrive?"

"The trains, the men at Hoddmimirwald Bunker said that trains two through eighteen never arrived! Train three says they haven't even left Ost-Paris yet!"

If that was true, then it meant that the largest bunker in the entire system wouldn't even be at an eighth of its capacity before... "FUCK! We have to tell the Reichsführer-SS!"

The Obergruppenführer and his aide immediately bolted up from their chairs and ran down the hall, desperately trying to reach the stairwell. Even if they made it to the top and told him, how much time would they have to correct things? To locate the trains and get them moving? To seal the bunkers? Even if it was too late, a slim chance of success was better than sitting down and waiting for death.

At last, they reached the Reichsführer-SS's office, lungs burning and knees weak. They summoned the energy, pushed forward half on momentum alone, to sprint toward the doors. But as they touched the handle, they suddenly found the door to be flying at them, followed by a wave of searing heat, and then nothing.

title: RAD_EU.8.t
desc:
3 days:

...how to describe it? Words fail me. Masses of necrotic flesh heaped high outside the medical tent, burnt tissue and gangrenous bodies piled like paperwork on the desk of a rector. Every hour more come and there are fewer supplies for the rest. Cruel, cruel calculus. I must look tired, deafened, bleeding men in the eye and tell them there is no space for them and nothing in the way of sedatives. They come regardless. I must rest now.

8 days:

...there's not a hint of sedative left, nor medicine. All we have is our hands, and what little bandages we can spare. Trenches full. No means to dig another. Vomit and blood stain the gloves. They're the last pair I have. Another one died on the operating table today. She was with child, I think. I'm going to be sick. Why am I not already dead?

15 days:

Lost our third doctor this month. Overwork, sickness, exhaustion - despair? Running out of paper, will be quick. We euthanize patients regularly now. One of them was a child, around 6, her face half burnt off. She smiled at me as I prepared her veins. I looked in a mirror and I hated the image. I wish they'd take them all away.

24 days:

Last diary entry. I envy the dead. Felt under my armpits: purple lumps. I'll join Ma soon.

They were right, weren't they? God died in the fires that day.

options.name: No one is coming to save us.

title: RAD_EU.5.t
desc:
The pilot glanced out of the cockpit, listening to the hum of the engines to keep his mind from wandering too much. He knew that he was flying toward death, no doubt about it. But what choice did he have? Even if he turned around or survived due to some divine intervention, what would he come back to? Reykjavik would be a crater. So would Nuuk. And so would San Francisco. Everyone he knew and loved would be reduced to ash, whether he completed his mission or not.

A line of green appeared along the horizon, rapidly growing as he approached. He could see the grey blotches of urbanity sprawled along the coast, most of it concentrated in one spot. Bremerhaven, one of the Kriegsmarine's most important North Sea ports. He knew that most of the ships there had already fled out to open waters, but just like him, they'd have nowhere to go back to. The sky was soon filled with dark explosions and the ear-splitting thuds of flak cannons. He remembered his dad describing the sound of it (the Devil's Orchestra, he called it) during the Second World War, and now he would have a front seat to its encore in the brief hours of the Third.

They were almost over the city center when their luck ran out. A lucky shot knocked out two of the jet engines, and another shredded the rudder and tail fins. They were losing fuel and altitude, fast. The warheads were armed, but they wouldn't have time to get out of the blast radius if they delivered the payload. He solemnly turned to his co-pilot and said "Let's put her down." He got a silent nod as his reply.

Before he could entertain any residual doubts, the pilot pushed the stick downwards, feeling the plane tracing a shuddering arc closer and closer to the ground. The flak fire intensified, taking out another engine, but it didn't matter now. When the bomber fell to below a thousand feet, he flipped the switch-

And Bremerhaven was no more.

options.name: "Now I am become death, destroyer of worlds."

title: RAD_EU.2.t
desc:
There were those who died in the scorching blasts that wiped clean the old world. There were those who survived and persisted on. And then there were those who watched.

In the stars men sat and watched the world below blossom into glorious pinpricks of light, and then for the first time they could imagine, they watched the Earth fall to a twilight. The lights flickered and dimmed, and over the course of weeks and months they watched as one by one swathes of the land would be dragged to the darkness. The men continued their toil in the stars, for they knew nothing else they could do, and slowly they withered away in their shelter in the eternal darkness.

As the last man watched, he could see a small glimmer, as somewhere in the dark globe below the first cautious steps were taken to restore some semblance of civilization. The smile on his face was sad, filled with curiosity and hope and regret, and that smile persisted as he floated in his tomb for eternity.

title: RAD_RUS.33.t
desc:
Антон нервно перетасовал свои бумаги и подвинул микрофон чуть ближе. "Ты уверен в этом, Василий?" - спросил он в третий раз за этот день. "Уже несколько десятилетий никто не выходил в эфир".

Его собеседник отмахнулся от его вопросов. "Хватит жаловаться, Антон. Мы протестировали эти вышки, и они работают просто отлично, верно? Я обещаю тебе: мы нажмем на эту кнопку, и твой голос будет слышен отсюда до... ну, до того места, которое люди называют местом, где они живут в наши дни".

Антон издал разочарованный вздох и ударил по деревянной парте, за которой сидел. "Но... что, если никто не услышит? Что толку рассказывать им о том, что происходит там, где мы живем? Разве они не хотят знать, что происходит там, где живут они?"

Василий нахмурился. "Ну, конечно. Но мы еще не готовы к этому. И мы не знаем, что там происходит, пока не пошлем людей на разведку! Но если эта система сработает, возможно, кто-то еще там поймет идею и откликнется, так что мы тоже будем знать, что там происходит! Тогда мы с тобой сможем собрать всю важную информацию и передать ее с помощью наших больших и лучших радиостанций!"

Антон открыл рот, чтобы ответить, но Василий отмахнулся от него. "Хватит болтать. Итак, корреспондент Антон Сергеевич - вы в прямом эфире через три, два, один...".

options.name: Дорогие слушатели, добро пожаловать на вечерние новости!.

title: RAD_RUS.24.t
desc:
По степям и равнинам того, что когда-то называлось Россией, ходит много слухов и сказок, как до огненных дождей, так и после них. Рассказы о Сером кардинале Руси и его Черной армии, о Последней Отечественной войне и темных днях Хаоса нашли свое место в головах, передаваясь от родителей к детям и от друга к другу, над пылающим костром или электрической дугой.

Но нет сказки, которая вызывала бы большее благоговение и трепет, чем рассказ о самой России-матушке, покровительнице всех детей евразийских пустошей. Персонаж России-матушки во всех ее бесконечных воплощениях завораживал поколение за поколением, по мере того как открываются и увековечиваются новые рассказы о ее великих деяниях.

В одном из рассказов она была дочерью великого лидера всей Евразии, взявшим её под свою опеку и восстановив земли после того, как она была ранена в битве. В другом она противостоит всему разгневанному городу, чтобы защитить своего несправедливо преследуемого любовника. В далеких странах вокруг замерзшей Вычегды ее помнят за то, что она столкнулась с темным зеркалом самого себя, чтобы спасти свой народ от уничтожения, а в вымощенных песком землях южных ханов казаки со страхом шепчут о её гневе, если осмелятся вторгнуться на земли русов. Даже на землях Дальнего Востока ей посвящают себя служанки-щиты и возводят храмы вокруг ее чучел.

Действительно, по всей степи, лесам, горам и тундрам слышен зов Матери России, и земля, которую она защищает, всегда будет единой духом.

options.name: Слышишь ли ты на равнинах песню Родины?

title: RAD_RUS.22.t
desc:
Андрей проснулся от звука колокольчиков. Это был не маленький колокольчик, как тот, который может быть в доме, а гораздо больший. В местной церкви, его втором доме, звонили в колокол, и его звук эхом разносился по городу. Священник как можно быстрее оделся и побежал к церкви. Там его ждал единственный мужчина, который мог стукнуть в колокол, второй священник в городе. Наскоро поприветствовав его, Андрей спросил, что происходит, и получил простой ответ: никто не знает. Крупные города в регионе исчезали, и люди рассказывали истории о полном разрушении и хаосе, где бы ни происходили эти массивные взрывы. Однако священник думал, что он имеет представление о том, что происходит

Андрей схватил Библию и быстро просмотрел её страницы. Он читал стихи, которые мог вспомнить, о том, что у всех было что-то общее, что-то, вокруг чего они вращались: Второе пришествие. Настал Судный день Самим Богом, и те, кто служил ему, присоединятся к нему на небесах, а те, кто не сделал этого, будут гореть в аду. Держа Библию в руках, он подбежал к парадному входу в здание и в последний раз взглянул на город. Через несколько секунд он был ослеплен светом. В свои последние несколько мгновений он думал о своей семье, своем доме и, прежде всего, о Нем. Пришло время присоединиться к Нему на небесах. Было бы доказано, что язычники ошибались.

title: RAD_RUS.10.t
desc:
Слишком часто урожаи были плохими. Один неурожайный год - и люди проклянут, но после этого они могут жить дальше, сохранив горькое воспоминание. Два года неурожая - это катастрофа, но с ней можно было справиться, запасаясь продуктами и снижая налоги. А вот три года - это было опасно. Это означало, что что-то сверхъестественное наказывает деревню за ее грехи. Или, как шептались некоторые в темных переулках и таверне, за грехи ее лидеров.

Председатель местной партии Михаил сначала пытался пресечь эти слухи, подарив из своих собственных запасов трех прекрасных свиней для деревенского праздника, но жителей деревни больше интересовал тот факт, что он мог так легко подарить трех самых жирных свиней, которых они когда-либо видели, в то время как поголовье скота на их собственных землях было настолько скудным, что ветерок мог бы сдуть его. Борис никогда не считал себя самым социально наблюдательным из людей, но даже он мог видеть, что котел неверных решений может легко закипеть, если будут предприняты неправильные действия.

Вот почему сейчас он сидел посреди улицы с аккордеоном в руке и пел песню, которой его научила бабушка с юности. Аккордеон неудобно сидел в его руках, но старые привычки, выработанные с детства, трудно было разрушить. Быстро мелодия комиссара стала устойчивой, и его песня приобрела деревенскую силу.

Сначала жители деревни не понимали, что происходит, но потом старшие из них начали подхватывать куплеты. Затем дети, желая угодить, добавляли свои переменчивые голоса к гармонии. Потребовалось время, но в конце концов все в деревне, от старого Михаила до пьяных нищих, присоединились к хору.

Переговоры все еще продолжались несколько дней после этого, но огонь остыл, и жители деревни согласились с тем, что ещё одному году будет дан шанс, прежде чем будет принято решение о действиях. На данный момент все успокоилось.

title: RAD_RUS.9.t
desc:
Бункер был мрачным и унылым местом, куда была перемещена цивилизация, бетонным кошмаром с тусклыми краями и ровными пустыми стенами. Комиссар был удивлен, когда ему сказали, что если случится худшее, то именно он, и никто другой, будет отвечать за выживших в бункере А4. Оглядываясь назад, он полагал, что это было не столько повышение, сколько отодвигание его на второй план, чтобы майор мог продвинуть своего сына на должность полкового комиссара.

Но мир полон иронии, и комиссар был совершенно уверен, что ни майор, ни его сын, ни кто-либо другой за пределами бункеров не был жив. Крики этих несчастных душ, разрывемых изнутри последствиями ядерного уничтожения, все равно прекратились несколько месяцев назад. Он слышал их крики в мертвых помехах радиоприемников.

Нет, проблема, с которой столкнулся комиссар, заключалась в поддержании духа тех, кто был заперт в Бункере А4 вместе с ним. Те, кого отобрали за их навыки или кому повезло оказаться рядом со входом, когда завыли сирены, были живы, что давало им большое преимущество перед своими товарищами, но они становились всё более беспокойными. Он продолжал произносить патриотические речи, как только мог. Он напоминал им, что их выживание было обеспечено примитивными конструкциями комплекса (по крайней мере, пока не кончилась еда или не испортилась система водоснабжения), и что продолжение жизни - это и наплевательство на ненавистного врага, и почтение к памяти павших.

Но если быть честным, он не был уверен, что его речи приносят пользу. И если в Бункере А4 собственный комиссар сомневается в будущем, то что можно сказать о его солдатах?

title: RAD_RUS.7.t
desc:
Что значит "человек"?

Человек - это просто человеческое существо с интеллектом? Является ли он человеком потому, что может думать и чувствовать? Нет, ведь раб может делать это так же легко, как и любой человек. Его отец был рабом еще до того, как пожары затушили горизонт, он подчинялся местным офицерам и тому бандитскому королю, который в тот день был сильнее остальных. Его смерть лишь привязала его семью к тому рабству, к которому он был прикован при жизни.

Становится ли человек человеком по убеждению, по какому-то тайному знанию, что на самом деле он не связан волей другого? Его брат верил в это, вплоть до того момента, когда охранники избили его до полусмерти за то, что он заговорил и понял, что ничего не может сделать. После этого он продержался недолго.

Может быть, то, что делает человека человеком - это рождение? Какая-то магическая и непознаваемая сила, которая дает другим людям власть над другими? Но если бы это было так, то сын старого барона не работал бы здесь рядом с ним, полуголодный и без глаза. Нет, никакого освобождения свыше не было и не предвиделось.

Истина заключается в том, что человек выбирает. Раб подчиняется.

А Василий, младший сын Ивана, рабочий на рудниках, задумался о том, что пора бы уже перестать подчиняться надсмотрщику.

options.name: Ни королей, ни владык, только люди.

title: RAD_RUS.6.t
desc:
Он был уверен, что было время, когда все было не так мрачно. Если обратиться к самым давним воспоминаниям, когда царь еще был на престоле, а Бухарин был всего лишь еще одним членом партии, то он мог бы даже вспомнить, что испытывал радость от того, что мир движется вперед.

При Советской власти все было, конечно, сурово, но все же он продолжал идти вперед с уверенностью, что его народ пройдет через горький век к свету и радости. Затем немцы, небрежно, неуважительно, бессердечно уничтожили все, что он ценил, всего за одну ночь. Его семья погибла, его народ разорван - его дух сломлен. Но когда старый казак сидел на холме, глядя на огромные грибовидные облака вдали, что-то внутри него проснулось.

Когда жители деревни стекались к его дому с вопросами, он отвечал на них и организовывал из их ополчение, чтобы остановить неизбежные набеги бандитов. Когда через деревню проходила разрозненная толпа бывших солдат, некоторые из которых все еще носили форму исчезнувшей Красной Армии, он набрал тех, кто обладал хорошим темпераментом и духом. Когда закончилась долгая зима, армия отправилась в путь, чтобы принести мир на родину, давно охваченную войной.

Задача не была выполнена ни при его жизни, ни при жизни его преемницы, ни при жизни её преемника. Но в конце концов часть родины стала мирной и свободной от тиранов, которые так долго приносили ее народу одни лишь разрушения. На какое-то время. И на улицах того, что когда-то было Москвой, бдительный путешественник может найти заботливо сохраненную статую старого казака.

title: RAD_RUS.2.t
desc:
Старик сидел, как и много дней назад, недалеко от хижины на холме, на котором он жил десятилетиями.

Медленно он покачивался в своем кресле, а старый, битый радиоприемник стоял рядом с грудой книг, выкрикивая лихорадочные объявления о разрушении Германии, Токио, Лондона и Рима, а также Нью-Йорка. Даже со своего места на холме он издалека мог видеть изменение цвета неба - какое-то своенравное оружие, запущенное в русские пустоши. Без сомнения, немцы. Это всегда были немцы.

Человек вздохнул, вытирая слезы с глаз, глядя на старый красный флаг, который все еще висел на стене рядом с дверью.

Дрожащими руками он медленно вытащил потрепанную фотографию из кармана. Он посмотрел на фигуры на ней, тогда все они были намного моложе. Все они были на похоронах своего учителя. Прежде, чем все сегодняшнее произошло, он сыграл свою роль в этом театре разрушенного мира...

Старик убрал фотографию обратно в пальто и выключил радио. Созерцая далекое небо и вытирая последнюю слезу, он встал и вошел внутрь, прежде чем плотно закрыть за собой дверь.

Хоть далекие времена миновали, для всех пришел час расплаты.

options.name: История, которую нужно забыть со временем

title: RAD_RUS.1.t
desc:
В Сибири был холодный день, как всегда. Снег покрывал землю, скрывая грязь, которая никогда не видела солнца и походу никогда не увидит. Проходя по ней в сапогах и мехах, Артем со связкой птиц в одной руке и винтовкой в другой, смотрел на облака наверху. Они выглядели темнее, чем обычно, что было верным признаком шторма.

Стряхнув снег со своих мехов, он подошел к своей обветшалой хижине и медленно открыл дверь, осторожно положив свои вещи на стол.

После этого он остановился и немного задумался. Он зажег лампу, почесал свою собаку Сашу за ухом, включил радио, как он делал каждый день, и нахмурился, поскольку из него исходило ничего более, кроме статического шума.

Артем быстро начал перелистывать несколько станций, которые он знал, и не нашел ничего, кроме шума, шума и еще раз шума. Через некоторое время, он пожал плечами, ведь он ожидал, что старая наклоненная радиомачта возле столь же полуразрушенной деревни рухнет уже несколько дней и ничего нельзя было сделать. Внешний мир и все его чудеса всегда были для Артема лишь далекой мыслью, и, вздохнув, он в последний раз выключил радио.

title: The Long Winter
desc:
Cold. Hungry. Tired. Weak. These were the only thoughts circling Beatriz's head as she felt the radiation chip away at what little energy she had left. She had lived her life with the ever-present, dangling threat of the bomb over her head, but had never expected all the boasts and jeers hurled across the Atlantic to ever amount to anything, nor did she suspect it'd leave her like this. She was empty, she was weak - and her family was dying.

Or so she'd thought. As she felt her old bones finally begin to give in, and her eyes slowly shut with exhaustion - something just barely visible over the horizon shocked her to her core. People. A well-armed group of men were patrolling the city's ruins, bags and knapsacks filled to the brim with what loot they could scavenge. Some of it would be used, some traded - but all necessary. The group patrolled the streets solemnly, taking moments of silence in between their looting, as some form of solidarity with those lost. Perhaps they could help her - perhaps they could help her family?

They slowly made their march through the gutted remains of the city, picking apart what little it still had to offer, like desperate vultures to a rotting corpse, before finally reaching Beatriz. None of them particularly knew what to say at first, looking at her fragile, radiation-worn body like she was an anomaly. Small mutters of 'What do we do with her?', and 'We can't leave her like this.' were all Beatriz could pick up, until, suddenly the de facto leader put his foot down with a sigh.

"Boys, we're going."

That was all he had to say. Beatriz was shocked. She begged and pleaded for something - anything to alleviate her, and her children's suffering - if even only for a moment. But the group picked up momentum all the same, as if they couldn't hear her. She seized what little energy she had left and quickly snatched at the nearest ankle, in some vain, desperate attempt to draw what little sympathy could be offered. But all she was rewarded with was a swift kick, throwing her to the ground, leaving her recoiling in pain.

Beatriz gazed at the men walking off, cursing them with all her might until her lungs could draw no more breath. 'Murderers! Savages! Bastards!' But it was all for nought, they continued down the path all the same, and Beatriz could do nothing but sit there, feeling herself slip away into the abyss further.

options.name: The cruelty ate at them, but better that than the cold.

title: RAD_SA.2.t
desc:
Хотя Финал выжег большую часть Земли, небеса над головой остались такими же нетронутыми, как и всегда. Звезды мерцали в великом запределье, придавая миру прекрасный вид чуда ночью, даже когда цивилизация догорала под ночным небом. Действительно, когда огни Земли погасли, небеса стали только ярче по сравнению с ними, и впервые за многие десятилетия все великолепие космоса можно было увидеть из любой точки мира.

Со временем человек снова обратил свое внимание на звезды, сначала пристально вглядываясь, затем удивляясь и, наконец, совершенствуясь. Люди восстановили древние линзы или сконструировали их сами и начали составлять карты небес. В своих наблюдениях они начали замечать, что некоторые звезды, казалось, блуждали по небу, как космические путешественники, направляющиеся в неизвестные небесные края. Для них существовало слово, хотя оно было утеряно во время Финала, поэтому люди просто стали называть их Странниками.

В землях Анд один звездочет влюбился в одного из этих странников. Там, где другие лениво дрейфовали по небесам, этот проносился по небу много раз за ночь. Он устанавливал свой дальногляд сразу после захода солнца, чтобы наблюдать за его прохождением, размышляя о его природе и назначении. Была ли это какая-то меньшая луна, подобная той, что тоже смотрела на него сверху вниз почти каждую ночь? Была ли это просто еще одна звезда, наделенная неестественной скоростью какой-то божественной или, возможно, сверхъестественной силой? Был ли это ангел? Бог, наблюдающий за своей паствой?

Однажды ночью он получил свой ответ. Наблюдая, как его "Странник" поднимается на гребень горизонта, он с ужасом увидел, что он охвачен пламенем, его след невероятно быстр и приближается. Разлетевшись на множество горящих осколков, он с оглушительным грохотом обрушился на близлежащие горы. Мчась к месту столкновения, звездочет с благоговением взирал на странное и удивительное зрелище перед ним. Странник не был естественным объектом - это было божественное творение! Обломки комнат, проходов и непонятных инструментов были очевидны в его форме, но самой большой находкой была не сама конструкция. Они лежал внутри - скелетообразные останки небесного существа.

title: RAD_NA.85.t
desc:
Bishop Phillips quickly began to recount the small heads that crowded the bomb shelter. ...97, 98, 99... Where was James? He swung around wildly; panic seeping into his voice despite his best effort to control it as he called out for the missing child. It had all happened so suddenly, they had almost no warning about what was about to happen. It was only because he, Bishop Alexander Phillips, had made an old friend in the military from his days as young priest that they even had a warning at all. It was thanks to the selfless act of that now almost certainly dead man that he was able to evacuate his Sunday school program. And now, one of those children was missing.

He ran down the school's hallway as fast as his old legs would carry him, praying with each step that he would find the boy in time. Another student had told the Bishop that James had gone back for something. Was it worth dying over? Obviously not, but the boy was only six after all, nuclear war wasn't something someone his age would easily process. He had almost given up when he found the child, standing nervously in the doorway, seeming as lost and out of place as a frightened calf. He scooped the boy up and with a strength that burned his old body he dashed back the way he came.

He thought they would make it, it was only a little ways left. Then the ground trembled with a violence man was not meant to know. He saw the open door of the shelter, several children crowded around the opening. Bishop Phillips looked at the small, innocent child he held in his arms. He knew what to do. The older children caught James and pulled him in, sealing the door shut behind them. Bishop Phillips sat down, panting from the exertion. Despite what he knew to be coming, he smiled.

options.name: Which of you wouldn't leave the ninety-nine for the one?

title: RAD_NA.62.t
desc:
The weather is at the edge of a hundred degrees Fahrenheit. An old pre-war air conditioner lies in the corner. It drones and occasionally whistles a little, but the room is still sticky and humid. The market is dim and has a quiet rhythm to it, the clacking of shoes and the clop of horses just out of ear. He is an old actor, from the north. Every word feels carefully practiced, as if from a script. His accent has been trained out of him, but that heavy Downriver dialect still lurks at the back of his throat

"You see, back then, there was nothing. Nobody had a book. If they did, they certainly didn't know how to read. Me and a couple friends, found a library in this old library. Was stuffed full of books and all. We were good readers. Eventually, found a liking to these scripts we found in a bin in the back. They were going to be thrown out, y'know, before the bombs vaporized it all. Some by Shakespeare. He was the most famous of his time. Some by a few others. We started performing them to the settlement."

His eyes well up.

"The town, it was razed. All gone. My dad, he was able to get out, but the flu - it got to him. We didn't have much left. The oxen were dead, just laying there on the road, covered in blood and arrows straight through them.

He takes a puff from his cigarette. Since the Southwestern Trading company moved into the Arizonian Province, the pre-war imitators have gained immense popularity.

"So we picked up theater. Just walked around, performing Miller and Wilde and all the oldies. Do you know about Declan Roberts? Yeah, we even read a few of his, after we met him at an inn down by Jaredsmore. They said we were one of the first. Eventually got enough money to put together a carriage full of props and scripts. Still just us, performing the same acts, the same monologues, night after night. Times have changed. Now, you don't need someone to keep watch for bandits. The mountain towns all get regular news from the valley towns. It's different. Now, I'm stuck south of the canyon. Believe me, I'd love to be back out there, on the open road.

He looks down.

"But I got a family now, and they've decided to settle out here. No bother."

options.name: "I've seen enough in this short life."

title: RAD_NA.51.t
desc:
They dragged John down, further and further, to the evil waters of the old energy. Why was he here? Why did he come to the Atomicists? His mama always told him to not do such a stupid thing, that he would become like them. Sickly and sore and covered in rashes. The old energy made them that way, momma said.

He could see the reactor far in the distance, across vast open prairies, its vast open cylinder cracked and split by the fire from long ago. When he was a boy, he always dreamed of one day exploring that old ruined reactor. Now, he wanted nothing more in the world than to get away from it. Stupid, stupid decision.

The chanting druids dragged him closer to the water of the Glowing River, its namesake luminescence long since dimmed but no less deadly than it was long ago. He resisted with all of his might, but to no avail. The head priest, reciting an old sermon from an old book, dunked John's unwilling head into the stream. He opened his mouth to scream, but the warm water filled his lungs. Lungs which would never draw breath again.

title: RAD_NA.50.t
desc:
Once the fires of the old world had consumed it, few were left to survive against the cruelty of the ravaged earth. To stop themselves from a demise like those who didn't make it this far, they had to work together. It was this way for a long time after, and the presence of one another was all most of them had. They became like a family, in every way but name. It seems that it was not fated to last, and so they all went their separate ways, scattering like leaves in the breeze. Some went to the graveyards of old, crumbling towers of rock and metal, haunted still by the ghostly outlines of the spirits that once resided within. Others found somewhere fertile, with green fields to spread their roots and bountiful forests to tame.

In time, these memories faded and were replaced by new traumas, turning what once had been amity to deep hostility in an renewed cycle of bloody revenge.

It had been many years, and the great scattering had become nothing more than a legend, aggrandized and modified to the whims of the tellers. Family ties were a myth between the bloodlines that now populated the valley known as the Olieoh. There was only war, and the land was filled with naught but cruelty and misery, as the blood of a warrior and the tears of a mother were shed as if they were the same. It seemed the entire valley would be stuck in the endless cycle, as man fought man and brother sought retribution for brother.

Then came the Peacemaker, spreading with him hope and unity. He was aware that those who lived by the sword would die by it without fail, and that the only way to create something lasting was to do so without violence. The Peacemaker brought together the people of the valley, showing them what they were doing to one another. He showed them the fields in which they buried their dead, rows upon rows of the aftermath of mothers burying sons, who themselves had interred their fathers, who had most likely mourned lost brothers. As every village, every band of warriors saw what they had lost by choosing the spear, they found themselves agreeing with the message of peace. The Peacemaker gathered them all, and beneath a Bukai tree they buried all their weapons, for they would never use them on one another again.

options.name: The Olieoh people were united, and they were once more a family, like their ancestors before them.

title: RAD_NA.44.t
desc:
The Traveler rode his stallion alongside the decayed steelroad, the wood between its two far-stretching beams long since rotted into fragments. Ahead, there stood a building. Squat and slightly collapsed, it sat along the steelroad's edge. More interesting, however, was not next to the steelroad, but sitting upon it. A vast object, split into multiple interconnected pieces, enforcing its weight upon spindly looking metal wheels.

The Traveler was intrigued. He had heard of these curiosities before, 'Treyns', they were called. Massive steel vessels that could supposedly carry hundreds and move with the speed of the wind. Fantastical nonsense, he always thought, but there it was; rusted to bits but still intact. He pressed his horse forward to get a closer look.

The wormlike-vehicle was extremely long, at least 300 paces, and its vast steel body was segmented into at least quint carriages. The Traveler had to see the head of this metallic beast, and perhaps divine what Gods must have built it.

Dismounting his horse, the Traveler entered the head carriage. The entire compartment was filled with dials and levers and gauges beyond counting. On the floor of the magnificent machine, lay the shattered skeleton of a man, rotted clothing still hanging from its bones. The Traveler knew, then, that there were no Gods. Not any more. The one true god was mankind.

options.name: And mankind is long since dead.

title: RAD_NA.43.t
desc:
Finally, it was happening. After years of signs and shouting and little listening, what Keith had predicted was now coming to pass. Six of the Seven Seals had been opened, and now, as the Seventh would soon descend upon the Earth, Keith could witness the power and the glory, and embrace his Lord. The air raid sirens blared, so loud that the entire City of Angels could hear. He stared up into the sky, expectant, anxious, ready.

As he was staring he could discern, far away above the clouds, a black dot, trailing fire through the sky. It was happening; Judgement Day had come. Soon, Keith would find himself in the arms of the Lord, his God, and he leapt with joy. Unable to control himself, he began to run towards the streaking object. As terrified onlookers ran and screamed for their lives, Keith sprinted towards his perceived salvation.

Suddenly, an immense, awesome flash of flaring light overcame Keith's vision, and he was blinded. He did not care, for none who see the face of God shall live. Standing blindly in place, arms outstretched, he recited the verse to all who may hear it, "And the angel took the censer, and filled it with fire of the altar, and cast it into the earth: and there were voices, and thunderings, and lightnings, and an earthquake. And the seven angels which had the seven trumpets prepared themselves to sound. And I heard a great voice out of the temple saying to the seven angels, Go your ways, and pour out the vials of the wrath of God upon the earth."

And so the vials were poured, and Keith was no more.

options.name: Who shall be able to stand?

title: RAD_NA.41.t
RAD_NA.33.t
desc:
Time passes, and the world moves on from the Great Tragedy. New civilizations rise and fall from the corpses of old. Children grow into adulthood into elderhood before they depart to the Reverse Side. In twenty-year stretches, more of the past is reclaimed, unearthed, and eventually reused.

It began when a city in Turtleland rediscovered the speakpole: a nifty little piece of Old World technology that, so the Reclaimers said, uses vibrations in the air to send messages to another piece of Old World technology called the speakbox. Convenient for communicating with other people from distances away, they were envisioned.

Then the Reclaimers found an unusually well-preserved collection of "speakards" in Excavation Site MO-12. Pictures of well-dressed young men and women line their clearhard surfaces, with names like "Bob Dylan" and "The Beach Boys" hanging above their heads. Someone noticed that, placed carefully onto a speakbox's carrying slot, the speakards fit perfectly well.

Many times in human history had accidents resulted in monumental changes that altered its course. In this case, what happened was nothing less than a flowering of songs from mankind's better times in the present. Through this accident an integral piece of mankind's collective culture, once forgotten, now finds new life in an age of wonder and hope.

options.name: California dreamin', on such a winter's day...

title: RAD_NA.20.t
desc:
As the sun set below the horizon, a man offloaded the final can of fuel into the thirsty tank of a generator. With several aggressive pulls of a cord, the generator roared to life, emitting a steady whir. Not far off, a set of lights flickered to life, brightly illuminating a grassy yard upon which an intimate gathering of men and women sat beneath the light, alcoholic drinks in hand.

As the power brought the yard to life much like the daytime sun, a music player was hauled over to the gathering and in turn connected to an electrical outlet. As electricity was fed to the device, loud, upbeat tunes began to emerge from its speakers. The group reveled in the euphoria of the music, and the memories it brought. Memories of a world seemingly without woes. Memories of an easier time. For one last moment, the hardships of the world could be forgotten, as they faded away like the passing of a dream.

The group erupted in laughter as jovial stories from a world now lost were shared. They continued to down their beverages with unusual speed, enjoying the few they had remaining. There were little more to go around.

The tune on the music player changed, and a woman of the group greeted the song with a dance. With several of the group singing along with the familiar lyrics, the others joined in on the dance. Laughter sounded off once again as the short moment seemed to extend into an eternity.

The night dragged on as the sky glowed with the unobstructed shine of the distant stars. Empty bottles lay scattered upon the ground as the group sat now in silent conversation, reveling in the final moments of the old world. The lights suddenly dimmed, and came back to full brightness again near immediately after, as the music player grew quiet for a brief moment in tandem. The generator audibly sputtered and choked upon the other side of the yard, as the group were once again met with their reality, like vivid memories of a forgotten nightmare. As the generator offered its final cough, the lights flickered into indefinite darkness. Finally, seconds later, the music offered its final notes, and the group sat under the silent starlight once again.

title: RAD_NA.15.t
desc:
The child screamed into life at 11:57PM, weighing a good 7.6 pounds, sporting a small mane of blonde hair and two brown eyes. His mother held him adoringly, his father looked on with a smile. They hadn't named him yet; it was hard to name something so beautiful and wonderful and important. The radio in the hospital room played, smooth quiet jazz - it was all perfect. The beginnings of a family.

Then perfection came crashing down. The smooth jazz, in a heartbeat, cut to static - then a buzz.

"ATTENTION," it blared in a monotone voice, "ATTENTION. This is the Emergency Broadcast System. Take shelter immediately. Take shelter immediately. This is not a drill.

Repeat: This is not a drill. An enemy attack is being launched against the United States. Take shelter immediately and stay tuned to this frequency for further instructions."

The nameless child woke and began to sob, sooned joined by his mother. The man's heart leapt into his throat. Not now. Why did it have to be now? He slumped into his seat, cradling his head in his hands for a moment. He knew she couldn't move, and he knew he would never leave either of them here.

The mother whispered quiet assurances to her son with no name as the father slid into the bed, wrapping his arms around his wife and son, tears streaming down his face.

The child cooed and giggled at his parents' faces, and as his hand curled around his mother's pinky, a blinding flash set the world ablaze.

Years later, scavengers would find the silhouettes of a man, a woman, and a child in the ruins of a hospital.

options.name: All this for lines on a map.

title: RAD_NA.8.t
desc:
Father Jacobs sat in his old white rocking chair, a contented smile across his face. Today had been a good day, and for that he praised the Lord. He watched from the top of the hill his church sat upon, down at the lights of the city far, far away. It was so peaceful on these nights, enough for him to forget the constant fear and anxiety that permeated every facet of the last few months. There was no worry about war tonight, only the comforts of freedom and the comforts of the Lord.

He didn't see the bombers, but he heard them. He thought they must have been from the airport at first--but planes never flew over his hill. Then he thought it was a military exercise. They did seem to be on the highest alert lately. Maybe it was...

The flash cut him off.

He flung his hands in front of his eyes and fell backwards out of his chair, lying in the dirt for a moment, blinking fitfully in a futile attempt to clear the blinding white haze that obscured his vision. He wanted so badly to simply lie there forever, to not look upon what awaited him, but he knew that he had to do it. He wearily brought himself to his feet, quaking fearfully, and waited until his eyesight had cleared. What he saw before him caused his heart to drop to his stomach.

The cloud was the first thing he noticed. They hadn't been lying when they said it was like a mushroom. It was exactly like one, really, but made of fire, dreadful fire, and a thick black smoke that could blot out the sun. He looked down, and all that was before him was rubble and fire.

This was hell, he realized then. It had to be hell. How could a God be good and allow this? He sank to his knees as he watched, thinking of the families he attended. He thought of the children--how terrified they must have been, in their final moments, before they were consumed by that damned fire.

The ground quaked beneath him as the smoke rushed towards him from the horizon, but he didn't care. The nightmare would be over soon.

As hellfire washed over Father Jacobs, he cursed God for letting his children die so cruelly.

options.name: Faith cannot escape the flames of Hell.

title: RAD_NA.2.t
desc:
In a great bunker named simply D1, many hid in fear as the world above them was torn to the ground. The people of D1 would live for years, and years, before slowly they began to leave.

Disagreements and arguments caused the first ten to go, ten of the original group, and they were followed by twenty, and more and more of D1's people began to drift away. Years would pass, before the final remaining survivors of D1, and their children, would leave the bunker. Their children named themselves for the city that D1 sat under, Cheyenne, and would form a tribe, traveling across the plains of what was once America, once more learning to train and ride the horses that rode free, and hunt the Buffalo and other native animals.

They would, many years from then, come into conflict with other tribes, from outside the Plains, or descended from D1. Across America the Cheyenne would travel, forming federations, warring with other tribes, hunting for their food, and exploring what people claim was once a civilization. To them, it was simply another passing reminder that where they rode, their people had, in one way or another, for generations.

title: Summary of the Deindustrialization Action in Helsinki
desc:
1. Dispatch a certain scale of armed personnel to factories in the Helsinki region, such as **Outokumpu Steelworks**, **Wärtsilä Marine Power**, **Kemira Chemical Group**, and **Patria Aviation Factory**, to maintain order and prevent sabotage.
2. Establish a Special Interrogation Team to question factory management personnel to obtain statistics on personnel and equipment, inventory machinery and means of production suitable for rail transport, and classify and grade Finnish technical personnel.
3. Alliance industrial backbone personnel and Finnish technical personnel are responsible for dismantling machinery and equipment, while Finnish prisoners of war are used to transport containers and heavy equipment.
4. Control and manage the families of Finnish technical personnel, and execute uncontrollable individuals.
5. Commandeer the local railway system; dismantled equipment and materials are to be transferred from Helsinki to Arkhangelsk, and subsequently moved to industrial bases east of the Ural Mountains.
6. Provide appropriate resettlement for Finnish technical personnel, including setting up barracks and distributing food.
7. Following the operation's conclusion, sapper teams are to carry out total **mechanical destruction, explosive demolition, and chemical contamination** of any equipment and material that could not be moved.

title: The Double-Headed Eagle on the Snow
desc:
This year, winter came exceptionally early and cold to Finland. Emil Koivunen stepped on knee-deep snow, his axe striking the frozen spruce trunk with a dull *thud*. His breath condensed into white frost on his eyebrows, and every inhale felt like swallowing ice shards. He looked up at the grey sky; Finland's sky was usually clear, but now it was veiled in an ominous, grey haze.

Suddenly, a piercing siren tore through the air. Emil knew something was wrong and sprinted home, then hurried with his wife, Liisa, and children into the cellar. Outside, there was no expected roar of explosions, only a deathly silence, and a chilling *hiss* like a venomous snake spreading over the land. Closely following, a strange, subtly yellowish-green mist crept silently and swiftly along the snow's surface from the edge of the forest, engulfing everything. Clearly, this was man-made poison gas! Emil peered cautiously through the cellar door crack, seeing his neighbor, old Jonas, stumble out of his house, only to fall heavily into the snow after a few steps like a piece of dead wood, his body violently convulsing. Emil faintly heard a terrifying gurgling sound from his throat, like a drowning man. The old man's skin quickly erupted in hideous blisters, and he soon stopped moving.

An unknown time passed, and silence reigned. The air in the cellar was suffocatingly foul. Emil carefully pushed the door open slightly. Outside was terrifyingly quiet, only the wind moaning. Stiff corpses were scattered on the snow, their postures twisted in agony.

The sound of heavy leather boots crunching the snow grew nearer. There were three men, all wearing unfamiliar dark grey greatcoats, but the striking **golden double-headed eagle** insignia on their armbands declared their identity. The leader's vulture-like eyes fixed on Emil's gaze. Unfortunately, a soldier discovered the cellar entrance. He pulled out a strange-looking instrument, operated it twice, and seemingly detected people underground. The soldier gestured, and several dark gun muzzles were instantly pointed at them.

"Out! Finnish pig!" the soldier motioned for Emil to come out. Emil, his wife, and children trembled as they crawled out of the cellar and stood on the cold snow. The soldiers were expressionless, looking at them like livestock waiting for slaughter. One of them, whose gaze fell upon Liisa's pale but still beautiful face, let slip a chilling, cruel sneer. He unhooked the canteen from his waist, unscrewed the cap, and poured a little of the liquid onto the snow. Instantly, a pungent chemical odor wafted up. He squatted down and, using his gloved hand, scooped up a handful of filthy, chemically-tainted melted snow and **brutally smeared it onto Liisa's face**.

Liisa let out a short scream; her skin instantly burned and turned red. The soldier studied her pain, watching Emil's face contort with fury and despair, a muffled, satisfied laugh rumbling in his throat. Emil's eyes were bloodshot; he tried to lunge but was stopped by another cold rifle barrel pressing against his forehead. After what seemed like an age, Liisa gradually lost life. Apparently satisfied with their expressions of despair, the man waved his hand.

title: Vengeance Thirty Years Later
desc:
Lakes. The forests and lakes of Karelia had never been this lively in thirty years. It was here, once upon a time, that Finnish traitors, along with Teutonic planes and tanks, began the invasion. Thirty years have passed—enough time for a generation to grow from innocent children to rifle-carrying soldiers.

After the battle, black-clad soldiers escorted a column of young Finnish prisoners of war. They marched in three ranks, heads bowed, over muddy, icy ground, their feet worn with blood blisters, their clothes soaked through by the cold rain. If someone couldn't walk, the black-clad soldiers pulled him from the line and **executed him on the spot**, leaving the corpse behind.

They passed through deserted villages, glimpsing houses with walls covered in curses written in Russian, like a tourist's "So-and-so was here." Underneath the walls were piles of corpses, some burned, throats slit, or torn apart by bullets. Several others, men and women, old and young, lay naked and piled together, with purplish faces and grotesque smiles, like a heap of long-uncleaned garbage.

After an unknown number of days, they arrived at a **temporary internment camp** surrounded by barbed wire. Here, the officers of the black-clad soldiers inspected each prisoner: only those who could **remain standing after a severe punch** were kept. They would later be transported by train to Onega and then to military factories in the rear.

"Drown the rest of these in the lake. Next batch."

options.name: The sons shall pay for the fathers' debts.

title: Good Man or Bad Man?
desc:
Grisha's rough, warm fingers tightly gripped the cold Mosin-Nagant rifle stock. Around him, the roar of the crowd surged in waves: "Let the Teutonic pigs pay their blood debt!", and Grisha's chest heaved with emotion—look, this was the strength of the Slavic nation! He felt the whip marks left by the German foreman when he was still a slave, faintly burning beneath his ribs, and blood rushed to his head; he was even a little dizzy with excitement. The **Black League** had brought the "**Great Trial**"; they had shattered the shackles of the so-called "New Order" and brought freedom, reeking of blood!

Several people in old German-style clothes were shoved out, their faces ashen. Grisha's gaze locked onto one old man—**Von Erich**, a German language teacher before the war. When Grisha was ten, he had been struck on the palm with a ruler by him for mispronouncing an "R." The memory of humiliation instantly ignited the flame in Grisha's eyes. It was him! These high and mighty "master race" people—who were they to insult him like this?!

An officer wearing the double-headed eagle armband roared from the wooden platform, enumerating the Germans' sins: "For Mother Russia! Execute the judgment!" Grisha's column was pushed forward. Mechanically, he raised his rifle, and the cold sight framed Von Erich's panicked face. The old man's cloudy eyes seemed to recognize him, flashing a hint of surprise, his lips moving silently. Grisha's finger rested on the trigger; he wanted to scrutinize this arrogant face...

"**Aim!**" the command thundered. But Grisha's breathing suddenly stopped. The face in the sight overlapped with a fragment of memory: this was not the ferocious face of the foreman, nor the cold, cruel face of the SS, but just the **desperate, terrified face of an old man** in an ill-fitting old suit, trembling with fear—this old man had also once frowned and tossed him an aspirin when he had a high fever. Although the old man's face always carried an expression of disgust when facing him, as if giving charity... he also remembered one time when he was beaten raw by a Wehrmacht officer, and the old man had tossed him a bottle of antiseptic. The memories instantly extinguished his boiling fervor.

"**Fire!**"

"*Bang—*"

Grisha stood still. In a daze, the old man had already fallen into a pool of blood. His rifle-holding hand was trembling uncontrollably. All around were the celebrating crowds and the shouts of "**Long live the Great Trial!**" He opened his mouth, but his throat felt blocked. His gaze moved past the crowd, landing on the corpse at the foot of an oak tree. A worn German pamphlet slipped out of the old man's pocket, falling into the blood. The stained pages were blown open by the wind, revealing lines of unfamiliar poetry—Goethe's *Faust*. A small doubt emerged in the bottom of Grisha's heart, which had just been filled with vengeful fanaticism: "**What if some Germans weren't that bad?**"

options.name: But he only dared bury this doubt deep in his heart.

title: Vengeance for Vengeance
desc:
"I curse their mother! How did these Slav bastards get here again?!" Inside a command post in **Moskowien**, a general roared into the phone. "You better prepare immediately to deal with these Slavic vermin! Oh, by the way, I'll ask the higher-ups to send you some more troops. You absolutely must catch those disobedient slaves in the factory and make an example of them, or we're finished! Did you understand?!"

Having said this, the general threw the phone and collapsed weakly into his seat, the **West Russian War** from over twenty years ago flashing before his eyes—that war almost crushed the vital colonial territory of Moskowien. Fortunately, the Aryan race was favored by heaven, preventing those Slavic beasts from winning. He was sure this time would be the same.

Thinking this, the general's tension slightly eased. He went to the mirror to adjust his uniform, put on his cap, and checked if anything was dirty or torn. He wouldn't want to command his soldiers with a messy face.

Just then, a loud explosion came from outside the window, startling the general, who staggered and fell to the floor. "What's going on?! Have those Slavs already attacked?" He stood up and looked out the window: yellowish-green gas permeated everywhere, and large and small corpses of soldiers lay on the ground. As a military man, he suddenly realized this was a **poison gas shell** or something similar. A wave of panic surged through his heart; he needed to hurry and inform others that those beasts had used **chemical weapons**, but it was too late. A shell was flying straight towards his location, and just as he picked up the phone, the shell hit.

"A beautiful shot! Kosov, I heard that Teutonic bastard in that house was an old general. Now they'll know what pain is! Hahahaha!" Kosov ignored him. He just kept aiming to himself. He could see how terrified those scattering Germans were, and he had seen the same fear—on the faces of his **wife and five-year-old daughter**. He could still recall the scene when his wife and daughter were executed by the Nazis. He had just escaped from a slave labor factory and saw two females, one big and one small, publicly shot by the Nazis. He pitied them then. But when he had a chance to look closer, he swore he would make these Nazi pigs taste what it was like to be tortured and killed. After escaping to the fragmented Russian lands, he was quickly drawn to the **Black League**'s ideology and became an excellent warrior.

He fired another shell, and a large mess of blood and rotten flesh flew into the air, but Kosov felt no fear. On the contrary, he felt a hint of... **pleasure**?

title: Redemption or Death
desc: "I heard you captured a batch of German soldiers?" "Yes, and we're planning to give them a good welcome." Inside a barracks, two Black League officers were talking. Not far from them, in a relatively hidden room, a group of people were trying every means to extract useful information from the prisoners, but despite clubs, electric shocks, and **ripping out fingernails**, the German POWs refused to disclose even a tiny bit of their unit's movements. "You really have guts, don't you? Fine, let me see how much guts you really have!" the leading Black League soldier shouted at the prisoners. "Someone! Take these dog-fucking Teutonic bastards to the wall. I'm not going to baby them anymore!" A group of tall men dragged and pulled the German soldiers to a dilapidated wall. Anger still burned in the eyes of the German soldiers; they seemed deeply unwilling. "Line them up! I have something to say to them!" Though troublesome, these 'gutsy' Teutons were persuaded to line up. "Do you know why I brought you here?" "Go fuck your mother, you Slavic bastard! I don't care to listen to your—" A gunshot interrupted the German soldier's roar, and he fell to the ground, lifeless. "You Teutons are truly ill-mannered savages. The name 'Germanic barbarians' is entirely accurate, wouldn't you agree?" The remaining German soldiers, seeing the increasingly cold corpse of their comrade, had much of the fire in their eyes extinguished. They mostly said nothing, just staring blankly around. "Alright... listen! Bastards! You might remember what your ancestors or you yourselves did during the war! I'm not referring to one specific war, but every single one! We know all about your cruel abuse of our compatriots! You Nazi pigs are the absolute lowest of humanity! And yet you call yourselves the noble Aryan race—nothing but a self-deceiving lie! I bet you don't even understand your Führer, just blindly worship him! Let me tell you, your so-called great Führer is nothing but a junkie who spends his days doing drugs, engaging in debauchery, and doesn't care whether you live or die! He only mindlessly sends you into battle! But he won't give you any benefit after the fight!" After a moment of silence, seeing no reaction from the prisoners, the Black League soldier continued: "I don't know if you're regretting or cursing, but it doesn't matter! I'll give you two choices! The first: join our **great vengeance undertaking** and atone for your sins. The second: perhaps it will make you seem 'gutsy,' which is to refuse to follow our orders! If you choose the second... Good! Now, those who want to join the **Redemption Brigade** and become glorious members, raise your hand!" A dead silence followed. The German soldiers exchanged glances, constantly wavering and deciding in their hearts. Finally, **two** German soldiers raised their hands.

options.name: “Take the rest to the gas chamber; let them have a good time.”

title: Inside the Factory
desc:
Just like any other day, Ilich was working around the clock in a **meat factory** in **German-controlled Moskowien**. He had forgotten how long he had been here—days? months? even years? He was now like an emotionless machine, processing parts on the assembly line every day. Seeing one compatriot after another collapse from overwork around him, he dared not imagine their fate—would they be saved, or simply thrown out to feed the rats? He didn't know.

But this Ilich was a disguise for the Germans. Months ago, he had secretly contacted a **partisan group** and helped them hide weapons. He and the partisans had been waiting for the right moment.

Finally, his chance came. When news arrived that Russia was united again and attacking Germany, he would never forget the look of terror on the faces of the factory guards. He watched their horrified expressions, struggling to suppress a sneer, and picked up a **wrench** nearby... "Striking the back of a person's head with full force can be instantly fatal," he recalled the lesson the partisan taught him. He implemented this test behind the guard, who hadn't noticed his approach.

The great test succeeded. He searched the fallen guard, finding a pistol and bullets. He shouted: "**Compatriots! Answer the call of our great Motherland! Stand up! Straighten your spines!**" Dozens of other workers responded, and together they killed the remaining few guards in the factory. Ilich immediately ran to their usual meeting spot to link up with the partisans, but the person who greeted him was a stranger wearing a **black uniform** and a **gas mask**. The man handed him a gas mask, introducing himself as a soldier of the "**Black League**," now engaged in the great vengeance undertaking against the Teutons. Ilich immediately understood what he meant and led the Black League soldier to the warehouse where he usually stored weapons.

options.name: “Distribute these rifles later. Your time has come.”

title: An Ordinary Day
desc:
"How many days have I been here?" Hans mused to himself. Many months ago, he was taken in by the Black League as a German prisoner of war into a unit seemingly called the **Redemption Brigade**. In this unit, he was not treated as a regular soldier; instead, he seemed more like an object to be used and discarded.

And that was indeed the truth. One afternoon, Hans's company was required to assist a Black League regular army unit in a combat mission, and the task assigned to him was... "Fucking **human mine detector**? Is the person who gave this order an idiot?" Hans cursed fiercely in his heart when he heard his mission.

"I can see that some of you might have opinions! Don't forget! This is what you deserve! We will never forget the cruelty you Teutons inflicted upon our Slavic compatriots! If any of you dare to disobey orders, we will throw you directly onto a landmine!" The captain of the Redemption Brigade shouted at them. Hans glared at him fiercely, thankful the captain didn't see it.

....

Hans and his group were taken to a marked area. A wooden sign was haphazardly inscribed with: "**Minefield**." Hans wanted to open his mouth and say something but felt a rifle barrel pressed against his back. He immediately swallowed the words he was about to say and cautiously stepped forward, detecting.

About ten minutes later, Hans was still alive. He lamented how good his luck was. But just then, he suddenly felt an abnormal looseness in the soil. He immediately realized he might have stepped on a landmine.

"**Am I going to die?**" Hans suddenly thought, but he wasn't willing to die just like that. A dangerous idea popped into his mind. He located the nearest Black League soldier, waved his hand to him, and tried to call him over. The Black League soldier seemed unsuspicious and walked toward him step by step.

"Yes, just like that..." Hans murmured softly. He estimated the killing range of the landmine beneath his foot, doing his best to draw the man closer without attracting attention.

Just as he was about to succeed, a gunshot rang out. Hans instantly felt his body go limp and he fell down.

With a loud explosion, Hans dissolved into a **cloud of blood mist**.

options.name: The little Teutonic bastard was quite cunning.

title: Oh, How Pure
desc:
"A bright, sunny day, isn't it?" Belikov said to a half-dead German soldier on the ground.

"Honestly, Teuton, if I were you, I'd have asked the great Führer to give me a gas mask, but he has to spend the money for your gas masks on **Pervitin**, right?" The German soldier said nothing; he was close to losing consciousness.

Belikov kicked the soldier hard. The soldier seemed startled, violently flinching and staring at Belikov with panic-stricken eyes.

"Teutonic bastard, do you know how the Nazis dealt with our great Slavs, huh?" Belikov raised his rifle, aimed at the German soldier's knee, and pulled the trigger.

"Fuck! Please, I beg you, let me go!" The German soldier screamed in pain. "Haha! Teuton! So you feel pain too!" Belikov slammed the rifle butt into the German soldier's abdomen, then dragged his body and threw it onto the street. A hissing sound of gas release emerged, and **yellowish-green gas** instantly permeated the street. Norton, the tortured German soldier, could only watch helplessly as his former comrades fell to the ground in panic. He, too, gradually lost the strength to control himself, and his vision blurred. "Mama..." he whispered with his last ounce of strength.

Belikov looked through the lenses of his gas mask at the Teutonic bastards gradually collapsing on the ground, the smile at the corner of his mouth becoming unstoppable. He used his rifle to deliver the final judgment on those German soldiers who still had a breath left.

"Oh, Teuton, you should thank me for ending your suffering..." Belikov murmured, pulling the trigger to execute a German soldier who was tearfully crawling forward.

As the yellowish-green gas filled the street, Belikov returned to his squad.

title: Chemical Warfare
desc:
One morning, Müller woke up. He rubbed his eyes, pushed open the door, and went to the ranch. He skillfully poured water and fed his livestock. After finishing all this, he returned home to prepare breakfast. While preparing breakfast, Müller looked out the window and noticed something unusual: some animals seemed to have fallen down. Unsure if he had seen correctly, he rubbed his eyes and looked again.

"Fuck," Müller whispered, then opened the door and rushed out. He watched as one animal after another collapsed before his eyes. Disbelieving, he rushed to the fallen animals, wanting to check if they had been hurt. Just then, he seemed to smell a very unpleasant odor. He looked up, glancing around, and observed a stranger in a **black uniform** and a **gas mask** not far away, writing something with a pen and paper. He wanted to confront the man about what he had done, but found he couldn't exert any strength. He was now lying helplessly on the ground, looking at his livestock, his life's work, but powerless to do anything.

"**The effect is excellent, Comrade Commander. That Teutonic farmer and his livestock were almost instantly knocked out upon smelling the poison gas, but I think we can strengthen the gas. That way, those Teutonic bastards might die faster. Report complete.**"

"Received. Inform all units. **Mass deployment of poison gas shells is approved.**"

options.name: Let those Teutonic devils see our power!

title: Biological Warfare
desc:
"Today wasn't much different from usual, except I was called out by the commander to look for nearby drinkable water sources. That sounds a lot like ancient warfare, doesn't it!

But the reality seems much crueler. Ever since my comrades drank the water I brought, they've been continuously getting sick. Some lucky ones survive, but they're basically no different from the dead. Some aren't so lucky. I hope this is just my illusion.

My commander called me over. He asked me where I got the water, and he was very angry. I was terrified, so I could only tell him the truth."

Albert stopped writing and followed his commander and a small group of people to the small ditch where he fetched the water. They took back some samples and handed them to the research team, anxiously waiting for the test results.

"I seem to have messed up. More and more people are dying. We just gave the water to the research team to investigate. I hope this is just my illusion."

But reality delivered a heavy blow. The report from the research team said they detected **various types of bacteria in the water**, all with extremely strong pathogenicity. Ingesting even a little bit could trigger various fatal diseases.

Sergei watched from afar as the German army frantically transported the sick or dead soldiers, a satisfied smile on his face. He reported via radio:

options.name: “Biological warfare is highly effective. We must rapidly develop more different methods of use.”

title: A Deadly Masterpiece
desc:
Lev used to be an artist, but after his wife and child were lost in the Great War that changed everything, everything changed.

Now, Lev is a glorious Black League soldier, a resolute commander, but at his core, he is still an artist. Next, he will introduce everyone to his most satisfying masterpiece:

"**Poison gas**. Fools regard it as a monstrous flood; they are scared out of their wits just by mentioning it. But we! The great Russians! We see it as a life-saving elixir! The Teutons in the distance are sick, craving to be cured by it. Just a tiny bit will let them be **reborn**!"

"But the great, loving Russians believe a tiny bit is not enough. They will send the **purest and most abundant poison gas** to the poor Teutons! Look, through the yellowish-green veil of the bride, you can see the ecstatic faces of the Teutons! They are overjoyed! They are cheering! They are dancing wildly! In that yellowish-green haze are countless dancers offering us the sincerest gratitude, thanking the Russians for their gift with the wildest dance!"

"Some Teutons are tired and lie down to rest. Look at their lovely, **infant-like faces**! They are sleeping like babies now, and great Russia has become their most loving mother, letting them fully enjoy the hard-won peace amidst the flames of war!"

"It was then that I suddenly recalled the ancient East, a country as old as Russia. It is said that an astonishing art, the '**Jingguan**' (Capital of Skulls), was once practiced there. I find this art to be as beautiful as its name suggests! I could no longer suppress the artistic heart that had been dormant for so long. At that moment, my heart trembled, and my hands wildly shook."

"When I finally completed it, I felt for a moment that **even death would be without regret**. Its structure is extremely simple, or perhaps a little monotonous, but listen, the individual grotesqueries and terror are its best seasoning! They are what give vitality to an otherwise boring scene!"

"I shall name it '**The Roar**,' my deadly masterpiece!"

title: Cloudy Liquor
desc:
The cold wind ruthlessly galloped across the Russian land, meeting every attempt to stop it with the most biting rebuff. No one liked this kind of weather, and neither did "Old Dog."

At this moment, he was fumbling his way forward in the heavy snow. He hadn't expected the weather to be so severe today. The muscles on his face had long lost feeling due to the ice and cold wind, only his mouth, still retaining some warmth, occasionally exhaled a brief puff of hot air, reminding him he was still alive.

But his luck wasn't as bad as the weather. After walking for an unknown time in the blizzard, he finally saw the small wooden cabin most familiar to him.
